papers.title: Progress Predicts Policy
papers.title_zh: 进展预测策略
papers.abstract: A task specifies how the world should change, while a policy specifies what the robot should do. We introduce Progress Predicts Policy (PPP), which learns a language-conditioned scalar field through the commands induced by its differential. We obtain action conditioning by composing a latent progress field with a shared world model and read its action gradient at a fixed reference command. Continuous commands scale this gradient by a learned positive gain, while discrete commands use finite differences of the same scalar. This yields a hybrid policy without a separate action head or iterative search. Fitting demonstration progress values alone does not ensure that action gradients align with expert commands. PPP trains the induced commands by imitation and uses double backpropagation for the continuous gradient readout to shape the field's local control geometry. Demonstration timing calibrates field values on observed states without additional annotation. The continuous readout remains learnable without progress labels but these timing-derived targets support progress monitoring during execution. Experiments in simulated and real robot manipulation show that PPP outperforms behavioral cloning under a shared architecture.

Abstract
A task specifies how the world should change, while a policy specifies what the robot should do.
We introduce Progress Predicts Policy (PPP), which learns a language-conditioned scalar field through the commands induced by its differential.
We obtain action conditioning by composing a latent progress field with a shared world model and read its action gradient at a fixed reference command.
Continuous commands scale this gradient by a learned positive gain, while discrete commands use finite differences of the same scalar.
This yields a hybrid policy without a separate action head or iterative search.
Fitting demonstration progress values alone does not ensure that action gradients align with expert commands.
PPP trains the induced commands by imitation and uses double backpropagation for the continuous gradient readout to shape the field’s local control geometry.
Demonstration timing calibrates field values on observed states without additional annotation.
The continuous readout remains learnable without progress labels but these timing-derived targets support progress monitoring during execution.
Experiments in simulated and real robot manipulation show that PPP outperforms behavioral cloning under a shared architecture.

(c) Measured action-space potential slices at a demonstration state show that progress supervision alone yields a gradient misaligned with the expert command (black).

Conclusion
PPP learns a scalar task field through the commands it induces: continuous commands from action gradients and gripper switches from finite differences.
Composing the field with a shared world model supplies action conditioning and an explicit chain-rule interpretation; direct action conditioning is also effective.
Progress labels are optional for learning continuous control, but calibrate the field for execution monitoring.
Under a shared architecture, PPP outperforms BC in simulation and on real robots.
Limitations.
Demonstration-relative progress may admit “arm clock” shortcuts based on arm motion rather than task-relevant scene changes.
The field has no Lyapunov guarantee, and its differential does not guarantee physical progress.
Progress-based recovery and sharing the task field across embodiments remain future work.

papers.title: Feedback-Linearised Trajectory Tracking via Model-Informed Robust Geometric DDPC
papers.abstract: Data-driven predictive control (DDPC) predicts system responses from recorded trajectories, but nonlinear dynamics can limit the accuracy of fixed linear predictors. This paper studies geometric robust DDPC for trajectory tracking of a fully actuated manipulator using model-based feedback linearisation. A mechanical model maps virtual acceleration commands into joint torques, while recorded data capture residual dynamics arising from imperfect model parameters. The controller minimises worst-case prediction error over an open Grassmannian ball centred at the fitted trajectory subspace. Simulations on a planar 2R manipulator under gravity compare the proposed method with double-integrator model predictive control (MPC) and direct regularised data-enabled predictive control (DeePC). Results show improved tracking over double-integrator MPC despite increased torque effort, while performance relative to DeePC depends on the reference trajectory.
papers.reason: 面向机械臂轨迹跟踪的鲁棒数据驱动预测控制
papers.tldr: 数据驱动预测控制依赖记录轨迹预测系统响应，但非线性动力学限制了固定线性预测器的精度。本文研究几何鲁棒DDPC，结合基于模型的反馈线性化，用机械模型将虚拟加速度映射为关节力矩，并用数据捕捉残差动力学。控制器在Grassmann流形球内最小化最坏预测误差。平面2R机械臂仿真与双积分MPC等方法对比验证了跟踪性能。

papers.title: RecallFlow: Episodic Memory as the Source Distribution of Generative Robot Policies
papers.abstract: Diffusion and flow-matching policies have become a standard choice for visuomotor imitation learning, owing to their ability to model multimodal action distributions. In memory-dependent manipulation, the robot must act on information that is no longer visible. Existing methods feed the observation history to the policy as an additional condition, while action generation still starts from Gaussian noise. However, the policy must then pick out the relevant target from a long and redundant history, leading to spurious correlations and unreliable decisions as the memory load grows. Additionally, the initial noise carries no information about what the robot has seen, leaving generation without guidance toward the remembered target. To address these issues, we propose RecallFlow, a flow-policy framework that builds the source distribution from episodic memory. Recall-Relocalization relates the memory to the current view through a few recall slots, so that the source reflects where the remembered targets are now. Recall Anchors then turns each slot into a Gaussian component of the source, enabling generation to start close to the intended action instead of from noise. The transport network then completes the action from the current observation alone, keeping inference nearly as cheap as a memoryless policy. We further build a suite of memory-dependent tasks grouped by memory load and compare all policies under a matched protocol. Extensive experiments show that RecallFlow achieves a state-of-the-art average success rate of 80.4% on the public MIKASA-Robo memory benchmark, and outperforms the strongest baseline by 20.3 points on our suite and by 18.8 points on four real-robot tasks.
papers.reason: 以情景记忆作为生成源分布的扩散与流匹配视觉运动模仿学习
papers.tldr: 在依赖记忆的操作任务中，机器人必须依据已不可见的信息行动，现有模仿学习策略把观测历史作为附加条件，但动作生成仍从高斯噪声起步，难以从冗长历史中定位目标。本文提出RecallFlow，把情景记忆作为生成式策略的源分布，用记忆引导动作生成而非无信息噪声。方法缓解了记忆负载增大时出现的虚假相关与决策不可靠问题。该工作为记忆依赖的操作模仿学习提供了新的生成范式。

papers.title: Old Experience, New Lessons: Relabeling Autonomous Robot Rollouts in Interactive Imitation Learning
papers.title_zh: 旧经验，新教训：交互式模仿学习中的自主机器人轨迹重标注
papers.abstract: Interactive imitation learning enables robots to learn from human interventions during deployment. These interactions naturally produce sparse human corrections and abundant autonomous robot experience without human action labels. Yet existing methods either leave this experience unused for action supervision or imitate historical robot actions, which can reinforce suboptimal behavior. To address this limitation, we propose Set-valued Relabeling of Autonomous experience (SeRA), a framework that learns from autonomous robot experience through set-valued supervision of policy relabels. Later policy checkpoints relabel this experience, and agreement across checkpoints filters the relabels. Since agreement does not guarantee correctness, SeRA constructs desired action sets around accepted relabels. Following Set-Supervised Diffusion Policy (SDP), it trains an action-chunking diffusion policy to increase the probability of actions within these sets. A step-masked denoising loss combines accepted relabels with available human corrections in partially supervised chunks. Experiments across five simulated manipulation tasks in online and offline settings show that SeRA improves policy performance over SDP and outperforms baselines that imitate historical robot actions or exact relabels. On a real-robot tomato-picking task, SeRA achieves 80% success, compared with 40% for SDP, using the same human feedback and training budget. These results demonstrate that relabeled autonomous robot experience can complement human corrections to improve policy performance.

J. Kober is with University of Stuttgart, Germany.
Abstract
Interactive imitation learning enables robots to learn from human
interventions during deployment. These interactions naturally produce sparse
human corrections and abundant autonomous robot experience without human
action labels. Yet existing methods either leave this experience unused for
action supervision or imitate historical robot actions, which can reinforce
suboptimal behavior. To address this limitation, we propose
Set-valued Relabeling of Autonomous experience (SeRA), a framework that learns from
autonomous robot experience through set-valued supervision of policy
relabels. Later policy checkpoints relabel this experience, and agreement
across checkpoints filters the relabels. Since agreement does not guarantee
correctness, SeRA constructs desired action sets around accepted relabels.
Following Set-Supervised Diffusion Policy (SDP), it trains an action-chunking
diffusion policy to increase the probability of actions within these sets.
A step-masked denoising loss combines accepted relabels with
available human corrections in partially supervised chunks. Experiments
across five simulated manipulation tasks in online and offline settings show
that SeRA improves policy performance over SDP and outperforms baselines that imitate
historical robot actions or exact relabels. On a real-robot tomato-picking
task, SeRA achieves 80% success, compared with 40% for SDP, using the
same human feedback and training budget. These results demonstrate that
relabeled autonomous robot experience can complement human corrections to
improve policy performance.
I
Introduction
Learned manipulation policies remain vulnerable to failures around contacts,
task bottlenecks, and states outside the demonstration distribution.
Interactive imitation learning (IIL) addresses these failures by allowing a human
teacher to intervene during deployment and provide
corrections
[
1
,
2
]
. These interactions
naturally produce two streams of data: sparse human corrections and abundant
autonomous robot experience without human action labels. Learning only from
the corrections leaves this experience unused for action supervision. We
instead treat it as unlabeled data and seek to learn from it alongside human
corrections.
Prior work has sought to exploit autonomous robot experience by retaining
historical robot actions as imitation targets. IWR imitates these actions
alongside human corrections
[
3
]
; CEILing uses additional evaluative
feedback to select useful behavior
[
4
]
; and
Sirius downweights pre-intervention actions using intervention
context
[
5
]
. However, autonomous actions need not be optimal,
even when they do not trigger an intervention or occur in a successful
trajectory. Retaining them as targets can therefore reinforce suboptimal
behavior. This raises a central question: how can autonomous robot experience
support policy learning without imitating imperfect historical robot actions?

Our key insight is that later policies incorporate additional human
corrections and may generalize these corrections to observations collected
earlier. We use the latest policy to relabel autonomous robot experience
and accept these relabels based on agreement across later policy checkpoints.
Yet agreement alone does not
guarantee correctness: multiple checkpoints can share the same error.
Directly imitating even these accepted relabels can reinforce prediction
errors through confirmation bias
[
6
]
. Learning
from this experience therefore requires supervision that tolerates imperfect
relabels.

(SeRA),

Conclusion
In this work, we introduced SeRA, a framework for learning from autonomous
robot experience alongside human corrections. SeRA uses later policy
checkpoints to relabel earlier observations and constructs set-valued action
targets around relabels selected by checkpoint agreement. A step-masked denoising loss
combines these targets with retained human corrections in partially supervised
action chunks. Experiments in online and offline simulation and on a real
robot show that SeRA improves policy performance over SDP and outperforms historical
robot-action imitation and exact relabel imitation in the evaluated settings.
Together, these findings show that set-valued relabeling extends learning
beyond human corrections to make effective use of autonomous robot experience.
Limitations and future work:
SeRA assumes that the desired sets around accepted relabels contain optimal
actions. Checkpoint agreement cannot guarantee this assumption, since later
policies can share errors. The current method also uses a fixed radius ratio
for relabeled targets and discards relabels that fail the consistency test.
Future work could adapt desired sets using checkpoint variance and use
observations with high disagreement to guide additional queries or robot
resets near those states.

papers.title: WEVO: World Model-Enabled VLA Optimization for Whole-Body Loco-Manipulation
papers.title_zh: WEVO：世界模型驱动的全身移动操作VLA优化
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) can improve vision-language-action (VLA) policies beyond imitation, but humanoid exploration is unsafe and simulator RL can exploit residual sim-to-real gaps. We present WEVO, a teleoperation-free framework for post-training a whole-body humanoid VLA in an action-conditioned video world model (WM). Simulated manipulation and locomotion play data improve contact-dynamics and viewpoint-change prediction. A VLA trained on synthetic demonstrations collects 20 autonomous real robot rollouts per task to align the WM with deployment observations. The VLA, whole-body controller (WBC), and video WM then form a closed-loop RL environment with dense progress rewards. Across three real robot tasks, play data improves every evaluated WM metric and downstream policy success; video WM RL raises mean success from 23.3% to 75.0%, compared with 48.3% for real robot RL. We therefore leverage the complementary strengths of both environments: simulation provides policy initialization and broad coverage, while the video WM offers a deployment-aligned environment for policy improvement. Project website: https://qianzhong-chen.github.io/wevo.github.io/.

Abstract
Reinforcement learning (RL) can improve vision-language-action (VLA) policies beyond imitation, but humanoid exploration is unsafe and simulator RL can exploit residual sim-to-real gaps. We present WEVO, a teleoperation-free framework for post-training a whole-body humanoid VLA in an action-conditioned video world model (WM). Simulated manipulation and locomotion play data improve contact-dynamics and viewpoint-change prediction. A VLA trained on synthetic demonstrations collects
$20$
autonomous real robot rollouts per task to align the WM with deployment observations. The VLA, whole-body controller (WBC), and video WM then form a closed-loop RL environment with dense progress rewards. Across three real robot tasks, play data improves every evaluated WM metric and downstream policy success; video WM RL raises mean success from
$23.3\%$
to
$75.0\%$
, compared with
$48.3\%$
for real robot RL.
We therefore leverage the complementary strengths of both environments: simulation provides policy initialization and broad coverage, while the video WM offers a deployment-aligned environment for policy improvement.

These limitations raise a central question: how should scalable synthetic data and limited autonomous policy rollouts be combined for whole-body humanoid VLA post-training without teleoperation? 1.
We build WEVO, to our knowledge the first WM-RL system for whole-body humanoid VLAs beyond fixed-base tabletop manipulation, coupling egocentric video generation with whole-body dynamics and dense progress rewards.
2.
We develop autonomous whole-body play data for WM mid-training: manipulation play improves contact-dynamics prediction, while locomotion play improves consistency under large egocentric viewpoint changes.
3.
We study how photorealistic simulation and a video WM can form a teleoperation-free policy-improvement flywheel. Experiments on three loco-manipulation tasks show that simulation provides policy initialization and broad coverage, while the video WM provides a more useful environment for policy improvement.
We design the system around two practical constraints: unconstrained autonomous play is unsafe on hardware, while RL can exploit residual visual sim-to-real gap in even a photorealistic 3DGS-based simulator. We therefore assign complementary roles to the two environments. The simulator supplies policy initialization and physically grounded play data; autonomous real robot rollouts align the video WM with deployment observations, making it a more faithful environment for policy improvement.

We presented WEVO, a teleoperation-free framework for whole-body humanoid VLA post-training. Its central design assigns complementary roles to two environments: the simulator supplies policy initialization and broad, physically grounded experience, while the video WM incorporates limited real robot deployment experience and supports policy improvement. papers.title: Improving Imitation Policies for Multi-Phase Tasks through Residual Learning Allocation
papers.title_zh: 通过残差学习分配改进多阶段任务的模仿策略
papers.abstract: Residual reinforcement learning corrects an imitation-trained base policy using a limited budget of environment interaction. In a task with several phases, this budget must be divided among the phases, and the phase in which the base policy fails is not necessarily the phase in which a correction most improves task completion. We formalize this distinction through the completion gain: the change in full-task completion probability when, during a single phase, a state-feedback controller replaces selected components of the base policy's action. We decompose the completion gain into the probability of reaching the phase and the conditional improvement in completion from the start of the phase, and we estimate it from paired episodes. The positive estimates determine which action components the residual policy corrects and how training episodes are distributed across phases. In stochastic point-mass docking experiments, most failures occurred in the final docking phase, whereas the largest completion gain occurred in the preceding channel phase; gain-based allocation improved completion over allocation proportional to failure counts and, in a variant with a longer approach, over uniform allocation at half of the budget. In simulated bimanual robotic assembly, the completion-gain estimates were positive only for insertion and release, although few failures occurred during release; in a second assembly configuration, a residual policy trained in the release phase improved completion from held-out states at the start of release by 16.9%.

A natural choice is to train the residual policy in the phases where the base policy fails. However, the phase in which a failure is detected identifies where the episode ended, and not necessarily where a different action would h

Conclusion
We introduced the completion gain to quantify how substituting a state-feedback controller in one phase changed full-task completion. We showed that under a common trajectory distribution through phase entry, the gain factored into the probability of reaching the phase and the mean change in completion probability from the phase-start state. We used paired gain estimates to select action components for correction and allocate residual training across phases. In simulated point-mass docking, we achieved higher completion rates with gain-based allocation than with failure-weighted allocation under the same nominal decision budget. In the longer-approach variant, we also outperformed uniform allocation at 250,000 decisions. In simulated bimanual assembly, we used controller substitution to select release for residual training. We measured a completion-rate difference of 16.9% from held-out release-start states and found no clear improvement from reset. We will investigate how training residual corrections in earlier phases affects the probability of reaching later phases and the probability of completing the task conditional on reaching them.

delta.quote:
In a task with several phases, this budget must be divided among the phases, and the phase in which the base policy fails is not necessarily the phase in which a correction most improves task completion. We formalize this distinction through the
completion gain
: the change in full-task completion probability when, during a single phase, a state-feedback controller replaces selected components of the base policy’s action. We decompose the completion gain into the probability of reaching the phase and the conditional improvement in completion from the start of the phase, and we estimate it from paired episodes. The positive estimates determine which action components the residual policy corrects and how training episodes are distributed across phases.

papers.title: CHAMP: Coordinated Humanoid Loco-Manipulation with Whole-Body Motion Priors
papers.title_zh: CHAMP：基于全身运动先验的协调人形机器人移动-操作
papers.abstract: Coordinating locomotion and dexterous manipulation is fundamental to humanoid robots operating in human environments. A key challenge is learning motion priors from diverse data and using them effectively for coordinated robot control. We present CHAMP, a unified framework for humanoid loco-manipulation that combines whole-body motion pretraining with adaptive feature extraction. CHAMP pretrains a vision-language model to predict future body and hand motion from approximately 2,298 hours of heterogeneous human and robot data. A shared motion representation enables unified whole-body motion learning across embodiments from datasets with body annotations, hand annotations, or both. To ground these motion priors in robot control, we introduce a Coordination-oriented Action Expert (CAE) and train it on replay data generated using the target controller. Through sparse routing, CAE adaptively selects, transforms, and fuses features from multiple layers of the pretrained model to jointly generate body and hand actions. In experiments, CHAMP achieves overall success rates of 84.8% on seven simulated tasks and 91.4% on seven real-world tasks with a Unitree G1, outperforming the evaluated baselines in both settings. In particular, CHAMP achieves 70.0% success on the long-horizon popcorn-serving task, compared with 40.0% for the best-performing baseline.

Abstract
Coordinating locomotion and dexterous manipulation is fundamental to humanoid robots operating in human environments.
A key challenge is learning motion priors from diverse data and using them effectively for coordinated robot control.
We present CHAMP, a unified framework for humanoid loco-manipulation that combines whole-body motion pretraining with adaptive feature extraction.
CHAMP pretrains a vision-language model to predict future body and hand motion from approximately 2,298 hours of heterogeneous human and robot data.
A shared motion representation enables unified whole-body motion learning across embodiments from datasets with body annotations, hand annotations, or both.
To ground these motion priors in robot control, we introduce a Coordination-oriented Action Expert (CAE) and train it on replay data generated using the target controller.
Through sparse routing, CAE adaptively selects, transforms, and fuses features from multiple layers of the pretrained model to jointly generate body and hand actions.
In experiments, CHAMP achieves overall success rates of 84.8% on seven simulated tasks and 91.4% on seven real-world tasks with a Unitree G1, outperforming the evaluated baselines in both settings.
In particular, CHAMP achieves 70.0% success on the long-horizon popcorn-serving task, compared with 40.0% for the best-performing baseline.

Humanoid robots hold the promise of assisting people across a wide range of everyday activities

A key capability is loco-manipulation, which integrates locomotion and object manipulation through whole-body coordination

Locomotion and manipulation are tightly coupled.
Body motion enables the hands to reach and interact with objects, while the demands of manipulation shape how the robot moves and maintains balance

These dependencies evolve throughout execution, requiring a policy to coordinate body and hand motion over time.
We therefore aim to enable coordinated humanoid loco-manipulation by learning whole-body motion priors that capture these relationships and integrating them into robot policies.
Learning such priors requires diverse examples of body and hand motion, yet collecting demonstrations on physical humanoids is costly and difficult to scale

Despite these advances, these methods do not jointly model body motion and fine-grained hand motion during pretraining.
This motivates us to learn unified whole-body motion priors that explicitly capture body–hand coordination through joint motion prediction, using heterogeneous datasets with annotations for body motion, hand motion, or both.
Translating these whole-body motion priors into coordinated robot behavior requires adapting representations learned for motion prediction to robot action generation.

Conclusion
To enable coordinated locomotion and dexterous manipulation, we presented CHAMP, a unified framework for humanoid loco-manipulation.
CHAMP pretrains a VLM on heterogeneous human and robot data to learn whole-body motion priors through body and hand motion prediction.
We introduce CAE and train it on replayed robot data to ground the learned motion priors in robot control.
This action expert adaptively selects, transforms, and fuses features from the motion-pretrained VLM to generate coordinated body and hand actions.
CHAMP achieves overall success rates of 84.8% on seven simulated tasks and 91.4% on seven real-world tasks, including 70.0% on long-horizon popcorn serving.
Ablation studies further demonstrate the benefits of motion pretraining and robot action grounding, as well as the advantage of CAE over fixed-layer feature extraction.
Together, these results highlight the value of combining whole-body motion learning with adaptive feature extraction for coordinated humanoid loco-manipulation.
Limitations and future work.
Our motion pretraining focuses on body and hand kinematics without explicit supervision of object dynamics or contact forces.
Control evaluation is also limited to a single humanoid platform with task-specific fine-tuning.
Future work will explore object- and contact-aware motion priors and generalization across embodiments and unseen tasks.

papers.abstract: Demonstrations show how a task can be completed, but differences in embodiment, appearance, and execution speed make it difficult to identify the guidance relevant to the robot's current progress. We introduce JEPA-ICL, a vision-language-action framework that couples predictive planning with demonstration learning. The policy learns to plan by predicting ordered future states in JEPA feature space up to subtask completion, capturing what remains to be accomplished. These plans guide action generation and locate relevant stages in demonstrations, whose JEPA-supervised content features provide progress-aligned context. Learning from this context, in turn, updates the shared policy that produces the plans and actions. This coupling connects anticipating the robot's own execution with reusing demonstrated experience. On the Imitator Game, JEPA-ICL achieves 80.0% seen-task success under C15 pretraining, outperforming Zero-WAM by 12.0 percentage points. Without contextual demonstrations, JEPA-ICL outperforms the VLA-JEPA variant without human-video pretraining, improving success rates from 96.1% to 97.6% on LIBERO and from 62.9% to 73.2% on LIBERO-Plus. With demonstration-based training and contextual guidance at inference, LIBERO-Plus success further increases from 73.2% to 75.2%.

Abstract
Demonstrations show how a task can be completed, but differences in embodiment, appearance, and execution speed make it difficult to identify the guidance relevant to the robot’s current progress. We introduce JEPA-ICL, a vision-language-action framework that couples predictive planning with demonstration learning. The policy learns to plan by predicting ordered future states in JEPA feature space up to subtask completion, capturing what remains to be accomplished. These plans guide action generation and locate relevant stages in demonstrations, whose JEPA-supervised content features provide progress-aligned context. Learning from this context, in turn, updates the shared policy that produces the plans and actions. This coupling connects anticipating the robot’s own execution with reusing demonstrated experience. On the Imitator Game, JEPA-ICL achieves 80.0% seen-task success under C15 pretraining, outperforming Zero-WAM by 12.0 percentage points. Without contextual demonstrations, JEPA-ICL outperforms the VLA-JEPA variant without human-video pretraining, improving success rates from 96.1% to 97.6% on LIBERO and from 62.9% to 73.2% on LIBERO-Plus. With demonstration-based training and contextual guidance at inference, LIBERO-Plus success further increases from 73.2% to 75.2%.

Demonstrations provide more than examples of successful actions: they reveal how a task progresses toward completion. To use this experience, a robot must relate the demonstrated process to what remains to be accomplished in its own execution, even when embodiment, appearance, and execution speed differ. This calls for a representation that supports both anticipating task progress and identifying relevant guidance. Joint embedding predictive architectures (JEPA) offer a natural basis for learning such representations through future feature prediction without requiring image reconstruction.
Recent work has advanced both predictive control and demonstration learning. JEPA-WAM
[
30
]
uses latent transition supervision for action generation, while HOST
[
8
]
connects demonstration localization with future observation prediction. JEDI
[
28
]
learns predictive representations for demonstration compression, and MUTEX
[
45
]
demonstrates the benefits of learning from complementary task specifications. These advances motivate a more specific question: how can the plan that guides a robot’s own actions also organize its use of demonstration experience? Future prediction alone does not establish correspondence across executions, while access to relevant context does not by itself ensure better planning. We study it through the state changes that remain before subtask completion.
We introduce JEPA-ICL, a vision-language-action framework that connects predictive planning and demonstration learning through progress-aligned latent plans. Our central idea is to describe an execution stage by the ordered state changes that remain before the current subtask is complete (
Fig.
1
). We learn this representation through a plan-conditioned Markov predictor, a latent world model that forecasts future states in JEPA feature space. The resulting plans support action generation and provide progress keys for locating relevant stages in demonstrations. Prediction and demonstration alignment jointly supervise these plans, connecting the ability to anticipate an execution with the ab

Conclusion
We presented JEPA-ICL, a VLA framework that couples predictive planning with demonstration learning. Supervised through recurrent prediction of future JEPA states up to subtask completion, its latent plans guide actions and retrieve demonstration context, while learning from this context updates the shared policy. Experiments on the Imitator Game show the advantage of progress-based retrieval over visual matching, complemented by LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and real-robot evaluations with and without contextual demonstrations. These findings suggest that anticipating what remains to be accomplished can provide a shared basis for guiding a robot’s own execution and organizing its use of demonstrated experience. Two questions remain open: our ablations test the plan as a whole rather than its design choices (intermediate checkpoints, recurrent transition), and we do not measure how training with context changes the plan itself.
LLM Usage Statement
Large language models were used in three ways in this work; the authors take full responsibility for all content.
Subtask annotation.
The subtask boundaries that define the progress targets of the plan were produced semi-automatically. Candidate boundaries were taken from gripper open and close events in the training episodes; GPT-5.6 (OpenAI) was then prompted with frames and the task instruction to label the segments and to place the boundaries that the gripper state cannot mark, such as the end of the corrective rotation in the real-robot task. Every segmentation was reviewed and, where necessary, corrected by the authors before it was used for training. No other part of the training data or the evaluation involved an LLM.

delta.quote: Demonstrations show how a task can be completed, but differences in embodiment, appearance, and execution speed make it difficult to identify the guidance relevant to the robot’s current progress. We introduce JEPA-ICL, a vision-language-action framework that couples predictive planning with demonstration learning. The policy learns to plan by predicting ordered future states in JEPA feature space up to subtask completion, capturing what remains to be accomplished. These plans guide action generation and locate relevant stages in demonstrations, whose JEPA-supervised content features provide progress-aligned context.

papers.title: Beyond Domain Randomization: Real-World Policy Adaptation in Learned Dynamics for Legged Robots
papers.title_zh: 超越域随机化：腿足机器人学习动力学中的真实世界策略适配
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning policies are often trained with static domain randomization for real-world deployment. However, real-world environments often exhibit unmodeled dynamic variations, such as payload changes or friction shifts, that lie outside the randomization distribution, leading to performance degradation upon deployment. We propose a framework that moves beyond static domain randomization by adapting a learned dynamics model to the deployed target conditions, with a concurrent teacher-student paradigm applied to both the policy and dynamics model. This framework integrates the dynamics model into an on-policy reinforcement learning pipeline, letting the performance of the policy align with the empirical target dynamics. Experimental validations on bipedal locomotion tasks demonstrate competitive adaptability under extreme physical variations, including a payload reaching 80% of self-weight and an oil-lubricated low-friction surface.

in Learned Dynamics for Legged Robots

Abstract
Reinforcement learning policies are often trained with static domain
randomization for real-world deployment. However, real-world environments often exhibit unmodeled dynamic variations, such as payload changes or friction shifts,
that lie outside the randomization distribution, leading to performance
degradation upon deployment.
We propose a framework that moves beyond static domain randomization by adapting
a learned dynamics model to the deployed target conditions, with a
concurrent teacher-student paradigm applied to both the policy and dynamics
model.
This framework integrates the dynamics model into an on-policy reinforcement learning
pipeline, letting the performance of the policy align with the empirical
target dynamics. Experimental validations on bipedal locomotion tasks demonstrate
competitive adaptability under extreme physical variations,
including a payload reaching 80% of self-weight and an oil-lubricated
low-friction surface.
I
Introduction
Fig. 1:
Overview of the framework. The pipeline operates in four phases.
(a) Simulator online pre-training, where a nominal policy is trained via
a teacher-student architecture, while a dynamics model is learned
concurrently using aggregated off-policy data. (b) Real world data collection
with the pre-trained behavior policies. (c) The aggregated simulation and
real data are used to fine-tune the dynamics model. (d) The dynamics model
creates a high-fidelity surrogate to fine-tune the policy against physical variations.
Reinforcement learning has recently achieved remarkable success in robotic
control. This success is largely driven by high-fidelity simulators that
enable massive trajectory rollouts and systematic policy
evaluation
[
1
,
2
]
. Within this paradigm,
domain randomization (DR) has established itself as a cornerstone technique to
bridge the reality gap, effectively handling modeling errors by exposing the
agent to a spectrum of physical parameters during
training
[
3
,
4
]
.
However, relying on a static
randomization range during training imposes inherent limitations when facing
significant dynamic variations. Fixed randomization ranges cannot fully capture extreme conditions encountered during deployment, such as substantial payload shifts or severe hardware degradation. Consequently, learned policies can either become overly conservative, sacrificing task performance to maintain stability, or fail catastrophically when faced with large dynamics mismatches
[
5
,
6
]
.
Alternative approaches focus on reducing the
reality gap through system identification (SysID)
[
7
]
or learned actuator networks
[
2
]
. While SysID
effectively leverages analytical physics priors to calibrate simulation
parameters, its performance is fundamentally bounded by the structural
assumptions of rigid-body dynamics. Variations that fall outside this
parametric family introduce structural bias,
and
additional interaction data cannot expand the expressive capacity of
SysID
[
8
]
. Learned actuator networks
introduce
neural flexibility to capture nonlinearities, but typically require dense
supervision from high-accuracy torque sensors
[
2
]
.
Moreover, as component-level models, they often fail to generalize to
system-level perturbations. Consequently, effective adaptation should benefit from flexible system-level dynamics models that capture effects beyond predefined physical parameterizations and can be learned directly from interaction data without requiring sophisticated sensing set

To overcome the limitations of static domain randomization
[
3
]
,
recent research has focused on adaptive control strategies through implicit
system identification. Rapid motor adaptation (RMA)
[
6
]
and its
variants
[
13
]
utilize a history encoder to compress
proprioceptive observations into a latent extrinsic vector. This latent
representation essentially acts as a proxy for system identification, guiding
the policy to react to environmental changes. More recently, Transformer-based
architectures have been employed to perform in-context learning for locomotion,
treating adaptation as a sequence modeling problem
[
14
]
.
However, these approaches remain fundamentally model-free. They rely on learning
implicit correlations between history and privileged states without
establishing a causal, predictive understanding of the system dynamics.
Consequently, when facing severe disturbances, these implicit encoders struggle
to reconstruct the underlying physical information, leading to reactive rather
than anticipatory adaptation. In contrast, our framework leverages a forward
predictive objective, forcing the policy to optimize against target
dynamics that explicitly respects the causality of physical interactions.
Learned Dynamics.
To bridge analytical simulators and real-world data, hybrid methods augment
physics models with learned components. Actuator
networks
[
2
,
15
]
capture complex motor dynamics,
while learned residuals
[
16
]
compensate for errors in simplified physics
models.
LIFT
[
17
]
adopts a hybrid world model that combines
analytical rigid-body dynamics with learned residuals to support
off-policy optimization.
However, its model requires estimates of privileged
quantities.
Using a fully learned latent dynamics model,
SimDist
[
18
]
performs MPPI planning,

Both limitations stem from their inherent design.
RMA is still limited with wide randomization range, such that the policy tends to be conservative.
SysID is constrained by the bias of identified parameters.
Our method has a 45.4% and 25.0% improvement of velocity tracking error
and 33.8% and 25.2% improvement of power
compared to RMA and SysID, respectively.
The reason is that our method allows the policy to converge to a
target-specific solution without the failure in a small randomization domain
or conservative performance loss inherent in
a large randomization domain.

Real-world locomotion under a 15 kg payload. Snapshots and
foot-contact sequences show that our method maintains a stable upright
posture and highly periodic gait, while Narrow-DR fails to support the
weight, resulting in severe body sagging and gait arrhythmia.
Fig. 8:
Real-world snapshots of the adapted policy.
(a) Outdoor walking with an added payload.
(b) Walking on oil-lubricated ground.
Under the low-friction condition, the friction coefficient of the ground is reduced to 0.25. Narrow-DR adapts poorly, slipping and
falling in roughly half of the scenarios due to
aggressive ground reaction forces. Wide-DR similarly has a crouched gait.
RMA manages to maintain balance
but also adopts a more conservative posture with larger tracking error and power.
SysID fails with coefficient estimation 0.89 under the same recorded data as Ours. This biased value significantly degrades the performance.
Our approach successfully adapts to the slippery terrain, maintaining
precise tracking performance and energy efficiency.

Conclusion
We presented a domain adaptation framework that moves beyond static domain
randomization. Instead of expanding the training distribution to cover the
physical shift, the framework adapts a learned dynamics model to the
target condition using offline real-world trajectories, then re-optimizes the
policy entirely inside the aligned model via on-policy updates.
Experiments on a bipedal robot under a payload equivalent to 80% of
its own weight and on oil-lubricated ground demonstrate the
effectiveness of this approach. These results point toward a broader
paradigm for sim-to-real transfer.
This paradigm has the potential to be
further improved as more real-world interaction
data become available.
Future work will focus on safe data collection, seeking to acquire informative real-world trajectories while minimizing risks to the robot.

papers.abstract: Can foundation models pretrained for generic numerical prediction serve as in-context robot learners? We investigate this question through tabular foundation models (TFMs), which are pretrained to infer input-output relationships from labeled examples in context. We introduce TabAct, which casts visual imitation as numerical prediction: frozen visual features and robot proprioception form the inputs, future action chunks form the targets, and each demonstration time step provides one labeled example that conditions a frozen TFM for closed-loop control. The predictor receives no robot-specific training or target-task fine-tuning. With one target-task demonstration available to each method, TabAct with TabICLv2 achieves the highest average success among all evaluated methods on both LIBERO and Meta-World, exceeding the strongest baseline by 20.9 and 5.8 percentage points, respectively. Additional demonstrations improve control without updating model weights: with five demonstrations, success reaches 94.2% on LIBERO-Object. These results demonstrate that generic numerical pretraining can provide an effective foundation for in-context robot learning.

Abstract
Can foundation models pretrained for generic
numerical prediction serve as in-context robot
learners? We investigate this question through
tabular foundation models (TFMs), which are
pretrained to infer input–output relationships from
labeled examples in context. We introduce TabAct, which
casts visual imitation as numerical prediction: frozen visual features and
robot proprioception form the inputs, future action
chunks form the targets, and each demonstration time step
provides one labeled example that conditions a frozen
TFM for closed-loop control.
The predictor receives no robot-specific training
or target-task fine-tuning.
With one target-task demonstration available to each
method, TabAct with TabICLv2 achieves the highest
average success among all evaluated methods on both
LIBERO and Meta-World, exceeding the strongest baseline
by 20.9 and 5.8 percentage points, respectively.
Additional demonstrations improve control without
updating model weights: with five demonstrations,
success reaches 94.2% on LIBERO-Object. These results demonstrate that generic
numerical pretraining can provide an effective
foundation for in-context robot learning.

Introduction
Providing a few demonstrations is a natural way to teach
a robot a new behavior. In-context learning (ICL) makes
this possible without task-specific parameter updates,
using demonstrations as context for action prediction at
deployment. Robot-trained in-context policies acquire this
ability through training on robot demonstrations and

In this work, we investigate whether pretraining for generic
numerical prediction can provide this capability.
The connection starts with the structure of a demonstration.
Each time step pairs an observation with an action, so even
a single trajectory provides a small labeled dataset.
Acting from a new observation then requires predicting an
action from these examples. Once observations and actions
are represented numerically, this structure matches the
prediction interface of tabular foundation models (TFMs),
which are pretrained to infer input–output relationships
from labeled examples in context
[
18
,
41
]
.
A demonstration can therefore supply the context for a TFM,
while the robot’s current observation supplies the query.
Can a frozen predictor whose pretraining uses no robot
data use these numerical examples to support visual,
closed-loop robot control?
We show that this is possible with TabAct, a numerical
formulation of visual imitation for frozen TFMs.
TabAct converts demonstrations into compact input–output
examples: frozen visual features and robot proprioception
form the inputs, while short action chunks form the targets.
Projections fitted on the supplied demonstrations compress
visual features and future motion, reducing the dimensions
of the inputs and prediction targets. At deployment, the
TFM predicts an action chunk for the current observation,
conditioned on these demonstration examples. The robot
executes the predicted actions, obtains a new observation,

Conclusion and Discussion
We introduced TabAct, which casts visual imitation as
numerical prediction for frozen TFMs, enabling closed-loop
control without robot-specific policy training or target-task
fine-tuning. On the evaluated held-out LIBERO and Meta-World
tasks, TabAct with TabICLv2 achieves the highest one-shot
average success among the tested methods.
Demonstration-conditioned goal switching, gains from
additional demonstrations, and effective control across
multiple TFMs and visual encoders support generic numerical
pretraining as a viable foundation for in-context robot learning.
Limitations and future work.
Our evaluation is limited to simulation, and inference
latency constrains deployment.
Inputs contain only the current observation; incorporating
observation history could support tasks that require memory.
An exploratory multi-output numerical model reduces
action-chunk prediction latency (Appendix
G
).
Future work should assess whether faster prediction preserves
control performance and enables effective deployment on
physical robots.

•
Frozen TFMs as in-context robot learners.
We show that TFMs pretrained on generic numerical tasks
without robot data can support visual, closed-loop robot
imitation through demonstration context.
•
TabAct, a numerical formulation of visual imitation.
We represent demonstrations as input–output examples for a
frozen TFM, using frozen visual features and proprioception
as inputs and compact action chunks as targets.
•
An empirical characterization of this capability.
We evaluate one-shot control, demonstration-conditioned goal
switching, and improvement with additional demonstrations,
and examine predictor choice and generality across TFMs
and visual encoders.

papers.title: Real2Worlds2Real: Scaling Self-Improving Agentic Real2Sim2Real for Robot Manipulation
papers.title_zh: Real2Worlds2Real：面向机器人操作扩展自改进智能体式Real2Sim2Real
papers.abstract: Scaling robot manipulation learning remains challenging due to the high cost of collecting real-world interaction data. Real-to-Sim-to-Real (Real2Sim2Real) offers a promising route by enabling policy learning in simulation grounded in real-world observations, yet scaling this paradigm across diverse tasks and physical interactions remains difficult. We introduce Real2Worlds2Real, a self-improving agentic framework that integrates scalable simulation-world construction with policy development. Given limited visual observations and task descriptions, its tool-orchestration harness constructs faithful digital twins and expands them into diverse, physically executable digital cousins. The agent adaptively selects tools and revisits construction decisions, using visual and execution feedback to refine geometry and physical behavior. Building on these worlds, the agent orchestrates policy development by coordinating data generation, policy learning, and refinement based on task requirements and simulation rollout feedback. Across both stages, the agent distills validated procedures into reusable skills that guide subsequent tasks. Experiments demonstrate improved world fidelity and successful real-world policy transfer, with performance gains from increasing world diversity and interaction-data volume. Skill reuse further improves world-building efficiency and long-horizon task success.

Abstract
Scaling robot manipulation learning remains challenging due to the high cost of collecting real-world interaction data. Real-to-Sim-to-Real (Real2Sim2Real) offers a promising route by enabling policy learning in simulation grounded in real-world observations, yet scaling this paradigm across diverse tasks and physical interactions remains difficult. We introduce
Real2Worlds2Real
, a self-improving agentic framework that integrates scalable simulation-world construction with policy development. Given limited visual observations and task descriptions, its tool-orchestration harness constructs faithful digital twins and expands them into diverse, physically executable digital cousins. The agent adaptively selects tools and revisits construction decisions, using visual and execution feedback to refine geometry and physical behavior. Building on these worlds, the agent orchestrates policy development by coordinating data generation, policy learning, and refinement based on task requirements and simulation rollout feedback. Across both stages, the agent distills validated procedures into reusable skills that guide subsequent tasks. Conclusion
We presented Real2Worlds2Real, a self-improving agentic framework for scaling Real2Sim2Real. From limited real-world observations, its harness constructs faithful digital twins and diverse, physically executable digital cousins, supporting adaptive data generation and policy development. Real-robot experiments demonstrate that policies trained in simulation successfully transfer to physical robots.
World-quality evaluations show that constructed worlds faithfully reproduce real-world appearance and physical interactions.
We further identify two complementary scaling trends: increasing interaction data improves policy performance, while increasing world diversity enhances policy generalization under a fixed interaction-data budget.
Finally, we demonstrate self-improvement in both world building and policy development, showing that reusing skills from previous tasks reduces world-building token consumption and improves long-horizon task success.

•
We develop
agentic tool-orchestration workflows
for both world building and policy development, enabling iterative refinement through feedback and cross-task self-improvement through skill reuse.

We demonstrate the transfer of simulation-developed policies to real robots, validate the visual and physical fidelity of constructed worlds, and reveal scaling trends in world diversity and interaction-data volume.

papers.title: One Phase Is Enough: Sim-to-Real Transfer with Direct Visual Reinforcement Learning
papers.title_zh: 一阶段足够：直接视觉强化学习的仿真到现实迁移
papers.abstract: Sim-to-real reinforcement learning (RL) has enabled impressive robotic behaviors, yet deploying policies directly from vision remains challenging. A common approach first trains a teacher policy with RL using privileged state observations, then distills its behavior into a vision-based student via imitation. However, the resulting student can substantially underperform its teacher. Directly training visual policies with RL offers a promising alternative, but learning task-relevant visual representations from scratch can be sample-inefficient, making one-phase visual RL intractable. We propose DRIFT, a simple recipe for efficient one-phase visual RL using image observations available at test time. Our key insight is to use frozen, pretrained foundation vision encoders, allowing RL to focus on learning control from existing visual representations. Freezing the encoder avoids costly backpropagation through the vision backbone, while its pretrained representations enable real-world transfer from fast, rasterized simulation rendering. Under matched architectures, observations, and compute budgets, DRIFT outperforms two-phase distillation and achieves a 58.8% relative improvement in average real-world success rate across three manipulation tasks. Controlled simulation evaluations demonstrate that DRIFT's relative advantage grows from roughly 9% in-distribution to over 61% under out-of-distribution shifts, suggesting that stronger generalization contributes to superior real-world transfer. Abstract
Sim-to-real reinforcement learning (RL) has enabled impressive robotic behaviors, yet deploying policies directly from vision remains challenging. A common approach first trains a teacher policy with RL using privileged state observations, then distills its behavior into a vision-based student via imitation. However, the resulting student can substantially underperform its teacher. Directly training visual policies with RL offers a promising alternative, but learning task-relevant visual representations from scratch can be sample-inefficient, making one-phase visual RL intractable.
We propose
Drift
, a simple recipe for efficient one-phase visual RL using image observations available at test time. Our key insight is to use frozen, pretrained foundation vision encoders, allowing RL to focus on learning control from existing visual representations. Freezing the encoder avoids costly backpropagation through the vision backbone, while its pretrained representations enable real-world transfer from fast, rasterized simulation renders. Under matched architectures, observations, and compute budgets,
Drift
outperforms two-phase distillation and achieves a 58.8% relative improvement in average real-world success rate across three manipulation tasks. Controlled simulation evaluations demonstrate that
Drift
’s relative advantage grows from roughly 9% in-distribution to over 61% under out-of-distribution shifts, suggesting that stronger generalization contributes to superior real-world transfer.

However, this two-phase process introduces two sources of performance degradation. Our approach, instead, directly trains the deployed RGB policy with RL. Furthermore, we examine the robustness limitations of distillation beyond the well-established realizability gap.
Efficient Visual RL and Frozen Representations.
Direct visual RL has become increasingly tractable with advances in GPU-parallelized simulation and rendering

We build on this approach for contact-rich manipulation, where policies must extract precise spatial information from visual observations.
Our recipe combines learned attention pooling over frozen patch features with fast rasterized rendering, reducing the computational burden of visual control

Conclusion and remarks
We present DRIFT, a simple recipe for efficient one-phase visual RL that combines frozen pretrained vision encoders, learned attention pooling, and fast rasterized simulation. These choices address the computational burden of visual learning while preserving the spatial detail that precise manipulation demands and the robustness that real-world transfer requires. By making such representations inexpensive to use, we free more of the GPU budget for experience collection, making it practical to learn transferable manipulation policies directly from pixels.
Beyond training efficiency, DRIFT transfers substantially better than the standard two-phase distillation pipeline, achieving a 58.8% relative improvement in average real-world success across three manipulation tasks under matched architectures, observations, and compute budgets. Although the two approaches attain broadly similar performance within the simulation training distribution, DRIFT retains higher success under controlled distribution shifts and on unseen real-world objects. These results suggest that directly optimizing the visual policy with RL learns more robust behavior, helping explain why its advantage becomes substantially larger when policies encounter the discrepancies between simulation and the real world.

papers.title: Ego2Real: Learning Bimanual Dexterous Manipulation from Egocentric Visuo-Tactile Demonstrations
papers.title_zh: Ego2Real：从第一人称视触觉演示学习双臂灵巧操作
papers.abstract: Learning dexterous manipulation from egocentric human demonstrations offers a scalable path toward robot skill acquisition. Vision alone, however, provides limited information about physical contacts and the demonstrator's force intent, leading to ambiguities in interpreting hand-object interactions. Capturing human touch via tactile sensing is therefore crucial for reliable human-to-robot dexterous skill transfer. We present Ego2Real, a framework that leverages egocentric demonstrations and tactile gloves to transfer bimanual dexterous manipulation skills to robotic hands. Ego2Real incorporates tactile supervision at two complementary stages: (1) tactile-guided hand-object interaction reconstruction, which uses measured tactile signals to refine hand poses and contact geometry; and (2) contact-informed reinforcement learning, which translates human contact patterns into robotic contact rewards. By combining refined motion references with physical contact rewards during training, Ego2Real guides anthropomorphic robotic hands to emulate demonstrated contact behaviors while adapting to their own morphology and actuation. Experiments show that incorporating tactile supervision into both reconstruction and policy learning yields higher manipulation success rates, underscoring the importance of enriching egocentric demonstrations with tactile observations to improve their quality and transferability.

Abstract
Learning dexterous manipulation from egocentric human demonstrations offers a scalable path toward robot skill acquisition.
Vision alone, however, provides limited information about physical contacts and the demonstrator’s force intent, leading to ambiguities in interpreting hand-object interactions.
Capturing human touch via tactile sensing is therefore crucial for reliable human-to-robot dexterous skill transfer.
We present
Ego2Real
, a framework that leverages egocentric demonstrations and tactile gloves to transfer bimanual dexterous manipulation skills to robotic hands.
Ego2Real incorporates tactile supervision at two complementary stages:
(1) tactile-guided hand-object interaction reconstruction, which uses measured tactile signals to refine hand poses and contact geometry;
and (2) contact-informed reinforcement learning, which translates human contact patterns into robotic contact rewards.
By combining refined motion references with physical contact rewards during training, Ego2Real guides anthropomorphic robotic hands to emulate demonstrated contact behaviors while adapting to their own morphology and actuation.
Experiments show that incorporating tactile supervision into both reconstruction and policy learning yields higher manipulation success rates, underscoring the importance of enriching egocentric demonstrations with tactile observations to improve their quality and transferability.

Overview of Ego2Real.
From egocentric demonstrations recorded with an RGB-D camera and tactile gloves,
Ego2Real reconstructs bimanual hand–object interactions with tactile-guided refinement,
yielding both a motion reference and a finger-wise contact reference.
These references supervise contact-informed residual RL for robotic hands in simulation,
and the resulting policies are deployed on real bimanual robots.

Introduction
Dexterous manipulation requires precise finger coordination and controlled hand–object interactions.
Learning from human demonstrations offers a natural way for robots to acquire such skills.
Egocentric recordings are particularly appealing
[
28
,
43
,
45
]
because they allow everyday manipulation to be captured with lightweight setups and allow demonstrators to perform tasks naturally with their hands.
Such activities usually involve two hands working cooperatively, making bimanual coordination an essential capability to learn from these demonstrations.
Contact plays a central role in this coordination: when two hands interact through a shared object, successful manipulation depends not only on how the hands move, but also on where, when, and how strongly each hand makes and breaks contact.
Yet egocentric visual demonstrations lack direct measurements of these physical interactions.
Prior skill transfer methods often infer contact states and locations from reference hand–object geometry
[
12
,
46
,
16
]
.
However, obtaining sufficiently accurate references typically requires high-precision motion capture that restricts collection to instrumented settings, and kinematic geometry alone still cannot reveal actual interaction forces.
Reconstructing hand–object motion directly from videos
[
18
,
31
,
46
]
removes the need for motion capture, but occlusion and depth ambiguity frequently lead to contact gaps, interpenetration, and unreliable contact estimates.
While tactile gloves
[
39
]
have recently enabled direct measurement of human touch for robot learning, most existing approaches
[
17
,
44
,
15
]
still pair gloves with external motion-capture tracking, leaving their role in egocentric bimanual transfer from noisy visual observations underexplored.
This raises our central question:
how can we combine visual information with directly measured human tactile signals to improve dexterous human-to-robot skill transfer when learning from egocentric data?
To address this question, we introduce
Ego2Real
(Fig.
1
), a tactile-guided framework that learns bimanual dexterous manipulation from egocentric demonstrations recorded with tactile gloves and an RGB-D camera.
Given a raw demonstration, Ego2Real extracts a

Conclusion and Discussion
We presented Ego2Real, a framework for learning bimanual dexterous manipulation from synchronized egocentric visuo-tactile human demonstrations. Human touch supervises two complementary stages: tactile-guided HOI reconstruction improves the physical consistency of hand–object motion references, while contact-informed reinforcement learning explicitly supervises region-wise contact states, forces, and contact establishment timing.
The benefit of each stage depends on the contact demands of the manipulation task. For tasks where contact-consistent motion references are sufficient for reliable transfer, tactile-guided reconstruction alone can achieve strong performance. In more contact-demanding interactions requiring coordinated grasp enclosure, force application, and contact transitions, additional contact supervision during policy learning provides substantial benefits. These findings suggest that human touch can guide dexterous skill transfer both implicitly through refined motion references and explicitly through contact-aware training objectives.
Ego2Real currently learns policies for individual demonstrations, relies on object meshes and simulation, and has been evaluated on two rigid-object tasks. Future work will explore goal-conditioned policies across demonstrations, more diverse objects and manipulation skills, and robot-side tactile feedback to further improve contact regulation during execution.

delta.quote:
Vision alone, however, provides limited information about physical contacts and the demonstrator’s force intent, leading to ambiguities in interpreting hand-object interactions.
Capturing human touch via tactile sensing is therefore crucial for reliable human-to-robot dexterous skill transfer.
We present
Ego2Real
, a framework that leverages egocentric demonstrations and tactile gloves to transfer bimanual dexterous manipulation skills to robotic hands.
Ego2Real incorporates tactile supervision at two complementary stages:
(1) tactile-guided hand-object interaction reconstruction, which uses measured tactile signals to refine hand poses and contact geometry;
and (2) contact-informed reinforcement learning, which translates human contact patterns into robotic contact rewards.

steps.quote: RGB-D observations initialize metric hand–object motion, which is refined using human tactile measurements mapped to MANO surface anchors. The refined motion is retargeted to OmniHand 3 while preserving interaction geometry. A policy is then trained with PPO using motion-tracking rewards and contact rewards derived from human contact states and forces. Human tactile measurements thus supervise both HOI reconstruction and policy learning, enabling closed-loop real-world deployment without tactile sensing.

papers.title: Reading Geometric Anchors: Viewpoint Generalization in Imitation Learning for Robotic Manipulation with RGB-Only Deployment
papers.title_zh: 阅读几何锚点：仅RGB部署下机器人操作模仿学习的视角泛化
papers.abstract: Moving the camera changes where objects appear in an image, challenging RGB-based imitation learning. A common strategy pairs synthesized views with the same demonstrated action, but ignores supporting physical correspondence across views. By predicting depth with camera calibrations, 3D policies may handle it yet suffer the issue of varied observed point sets. To address these limitations, we propose ReGeoAnch, a geometry-anchored imitation learning framework for viewpoint generalization. Specifically, we build global anchors in the robot base frame and local anchors in the gripper frame, providing shared physical references across viewpoints. Furthermore, Decoupled Appearance-Guided Geometric Readout uses Point-to-Anchor Aggregation (PAA) to obtain comparable and stable geometry around anchors beyond pointwise correspondence. A controllable and decoupled information flow, Anchor-to-Policy Readout (APR), leverages complementary visual and geometric information and supports viewpoint generalization: view-dependent appearances are queried by view-invariant robot state to select task-relevant anchors, with geometric values alone to form the final readout. We further introduce Cross-View Readout Consistency to align the directions of policy readouts from paired source and synthesized target views. Experiments on 12 manipulation tasks across MetaWorld and ManiSkill3 demonstrate improved viewpoint generalization over baseline policies.

Abstract
Moving the camera changes where objects appear in an image, challenging RGB-based imitation learning.
A common strategy pairs synthesized views with the same demonstrated action, but ignores supporting physical correspondence across views. By predicting depth with camera calibrations, 3D policies may handle it yet suffer the issue of varied observed point sets. To address these limitations, we propose
ReGeoAnch
, a geometry-anchored imitation learning framework for viewpoint generalization. Specifically, we build global anchors in the robot base frame and local anchors in the gripper frame, providing shared physical references across viewpoints. Furthermore,
Decoupled Appearance-Guided Geometric Readout
uses Point-to-Anchor Aggregation (PAA) to obtain comparable and stable geometry around anchors beyond pointwise correspondence. A controllable and decoupled information flow, Anchor-to-Policy Readout (APR), leverages complementary visual and geometric information and supports viewpoint generalization: view-dependent appearances are queried by view-invariant robot state to select task-relevant anchors, with geometric values alone to form the final readout.
We further introduce
Cross-View Readout Consistency
to align the directions of policy readouts from paired source and synthesized target views.
Experiments on 12 manipulation tasks across MetaWorld and ManiSkill3 demonstrate improved viewpoint generalization over baseline policies.

Abstract
Long-horizon robot manipulation requires more than predicting the next action from the current observation.
The policy must maintain a global procedural prior that specifies the expected progress of each subtask stage, while also tracking the realized progress produced by its interactions.
To this end, we propose RoboDemo, a demonstration-augmented manipulation framework built on Dual-Cascaded Test-Time Training.
RoboDemo accepts either a task-relevant human demonstration video or a semantically compatible robot video retrieved from simulation corpus as reference, allowing us to evaluate its applicability with and without paired human demonstrations.
Task semantics and physical motion information from the reference video are then transferred into persistent demonstration-intent memory.
During deployment, we causally compress online observations, robot states, and executed actions into interaction-progress memory.
To keep reference intent stable while interaction progress continually evolves, reference and execution video tokens independently update their respective fast-weight states.
The action expert performs cascaded memory reads, first obtaining reference guidance and then refining it using realized progress, allowing the policy to adapt to execution deviations without overwriting the stored intent.
RoboDemo achieves 90.7% success on Imitator Game and 73.3% success across three real-world household tasks.
Real-world videos, code and hf-weights are available in our project website.

Vision Language Action models (VLAs)
[

World Action Models (WAMs)

18

54

further enrich this paradigm by injecting predictive visual dynamics into trajectory generation.
Nevertheless, existing policies solve each control step from the current observation and proprioceptive state, and focus on short action window.
This locally reactive interaction becomes insufficient as long-horizon manipulation increasingly emerges as a central challenge in embodied intelligence
[
20
,
42
,
53

Successful long-horizon manipulation requires two complementary forms of knowledge beyond the current state.
First, the policy needs a global procedural prior that guides the entire manipulation process: it should specify how each sub-task ought to be executed and what robot states should be reached when that stage terminates.
Second, it needs an estimate of realized progress that records which sub-goals have actually been completed, and determines whether the current execution still follows the intended procedure
[
13
,
16
,
30
,
58
]
.
Long-horizon manipulation is not merely a next-action-prediction, but a persistent context construction over intended and realized progress.
Early VLAs
[
21
,
56
,
57
]
generate chains of thought (CoT) to precisely plan future motion trajectories, which serve as context to guide action generation.
However, text-only CoT does not fully specify the manipulation procedure.
Such as “place the object on the plate” does not determine the initial spatial layout, approach direction and relative gripper-object pose at contact
[
17
,
34
,
46
]
.
Subsequently, WAMs
[
6
,
18
,
25
,
54
]
alleviate this ambiguity by predicting future observations as intermediate goals and rec

alleviate this limitation by retaining future prediction as training supervision while generating actions without explicitly synthesizing future videos at test time.
Demonstration-conditioned in-context learning offers a more direct alternative: obtaining procedural guidance from demonstrations rather than predicting the intended future from scratch.
Representative methods, including ICRT
[
12
]
, Vid2Robot
[
17
]
and RICL
[
40
]
, use demonstration trajectories as prompts or retrieved context, allowing policies to adapt their behavior without task-specific fine-tuning.
Meanwhile, memory-based policies
[
38
,
53
]
preserve past execution through retrieved visual evidence or video prefixes to guide subsequent actions.
A reference demonstration, however, describes how the task should proceed, not what the deployed robot has actually completed.
To address this issue, RoboDemo constructs two independent memory mechanisms, enabling the action expert to benefit from both reference demonstrations and actual execution.

Building on this advantage, RoboTTT

20

Conclusion and Limitation
Conclusion.
We present RoboDemo, which separates demonstration intent and interaction progress through Dual-Cascaded Test-Time Training.
Cascaded memory reads integrate both contexts for action prediction while keeping learned policy parameters frozen.
RoboDemo achieves 90.7% mean Seen-task success on Imitator Game and 73.3% across three real-world household tasks.
Limitation.
RoboDemo uses fixed reference-sampling budgets and memory-register counts.
Adapting these budgets to task complexity and developing lightweight memory diagnostics could improve flexibility and interpretability.

Reproducibility Statement
The method and appendix specify tensor shapes, update order, gating, optimization, data conversion, seeds, metrics, and retrieval supervision. The reported C15/C30/C45 and Full50 results and retained retrieval-annotation counts are tied to saved experiment records.

papers.title: MXI-MemICL: Towards In-Context Robot Manipulation through Self-Retrieved Interaction Memory
papers.title_zh: MXI-MemICL：通过自检索交互记忆实现上下文机器人操作
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) offers robots a way to acquire new skills from a single demonstration without parameter updates. However, existing robotic ICL methods either rely on large-scale pretraining constrained by scarce, costly robot interaction data or require additional annotations yet struggle to generalize across tasks. To bridge this gap, we propose MXI-MemICL, a framework for memory-guided ICL in vision-language-action (VLA) models. By treating demonstrations as retrievable memory, MXI-MemICL enables in-context manipulation without additional large-scale pretraining or specialized annotations. Specifically, a visual-action causal encoder turns actions and their observed effects in demonstrations and completed interactions into reusable memory to guide execution. To retrieve experience suited to upcoming execution, an intention predictor forecasts the next stage's intent and uses it to query memory. The retrieved experience conditions the language backbone through experience-token prefixes and gated cross-attention, guiding action generation with a learned gate that regulates its influence. MXI-MemICL improves success over the baseline by +8.2% and +14.4% on RoboCasa365 and RoboTwin 2.0. Real-robot experiments show a +9.0% gain, with demonstrations adding +5.0% on seen and +16.7% on unseen tasks. The code will be made publicly available.

MXI-MemICL: Towards In-Context Robot Manipulation through Self-Retrieved Interaction Memory
Jialong Peng, Shihao Zhou, Feng Yan, Wen Xiao, Haozheng Wang, Wenqi Ren,
Wenyuan Sheng, Jian Qiao, Jiaxu Miao, Lin Ma, Chao Yang
1011.ai Sun Yat-sen University
*
Corresponding authors
Abstract
In-context learning (ICL) offers robots a way to acquire new skills from a single demonstration without parameter updates.
However, existing robotic ICL methods either rely on large-scale pretraining constrained by scarce, costly robot interaction data or require additional annotations yet struggle to generalize across tasks.
To bridge this gap, we propose MXI-MemICL, a framework for memory-guided ICL in vision–language–action (VLA) models.
By treating demonstrations as retrievable memory, MXI-MemICL enables in-context manipulation without additional large-scale pretraining or specialized annotations.
Specifically, a visual–action causal encoder turns actions and their observed effects in demonstrations and completed interactions into reusable memory to guide execution.
To retrieve experience suited to upcoming execution, an intention predictor forecasts the next stage’s intent and uses it to query memory.
The retrieved experience conditions the language backbone through experience-token prefixes and gated cross-attention, guiding action generation with a learned gate that regulates its influence.
MXI-MemICL improves success over the baseline by +8.2% and +14.4% on RoboCasa365 and RoboTwin 2.0.
Real-robot experiments show a +9.0% gain, with demonstrations adding +5.0% on seen and +16.7% on unseen tasks.
The code will be made publicly available.

Conclusion
In this work, we introduce MXI-MemICL, a framework for memory-guided in-context robot manipulation.
Specifically, MXI-MemICL encodes completed interactions into causal memory for closed-loop manipulation.
By anticipating next-stage intent, it retrieves relevant experience and adaptively injects it to guide subsequent actions.
By treating demonstrations as retrievable experience, MXI-MemICL enables robotic ICL without deployment-time parameter updates.
Experiments across diverse simulated and real-robot tasks demonstrate state-of-the-art success rates and effective adaptation to new tasks from a single demonstration.
