papers.title: DexWAC: A Unified World-Actor-Critic Model for Dexterous Robot Manipulation
papers.title_zh: DexWAC：面向灵巧机器人操作的世界—演员—评论家统一模型
papers.abstract: Robot demonstrations provide more than actions to imitate: they reveal how actions change the world and how those changes contribute to task success. Recent world-action models (WAMs) extend vision-language-action (VLA) models with the first signal by jointly predicting actions and future observations, yet this predictive ability serves only as an auxiliary loss for policy learning. Meanwhile, most policy improvement methods learn dynamics and values in separate models, increasing training overhead and limiting representation sharing between these complementary objectives. We introduce DexWAC, a unified world-actor-critic model that jointly learns an actor, an action-conditioned world model, and a bootstrapped critic in a single robot pretraining stage. Our key insight is that visual prediction encourages control-relevant features, while value supervision promotes task-relevant representations; together, they shape a representation suited to policy learning. Built on an image-editing backbone, DexWAC predicts, for each action chunk, the visual latent and proprioception at its endpoint together with its reward and continuation, so the world model alone efficiently yields complete imagined transitions without generating intermediate video frames. After adapting the world model and critic on real rollouts, we improve the pretrained actor through either PPO on imagined rollouts or critic-guided best-of-$N$ selection. DexWAC surpasses the large-scale pretrained VLA and WAM baselines in simulation and achieves 75% average success on two real-world tasks, compared with 45% for $π_{0.5}$. Its world model is more accurate and faster than video-based baselines, and ablations confirm that learning dynamics and value together improves the policy.

Abstract
Robot demonstrations provide more than actions to imitate: they reveal how actions change the world and how those changes contribute to task success. Recent world–action models (WAMs) extend vision–language–action (VLA) models with the first signal by jointly predicting actions and future observations, yet this predictive ability serves only as an auxiliary loss for policy learning. Meanwhile, most policy improvement methods learn dynamics and values in separate models, increasing training overhead and limiting representation sharing between these complementary objectives. We introduce
Dex
W
A
C
, a unified world–actor–critic model that jointly learns
an actor, an action-conditioned world model, and a bootstrapped critic in a single robot pretraining stage. Our key insight is that visual prediction encourages control-relevant features, while value supervision promotes task-relevant representations; together, they shape a representation suited to policy learning.
Built on an image-editing backbone, DexWAC predicts, for each action
chunk, the visual latent and proprioception at its endpoint together
with its reward and continuation, so the world model alone efficiently
yields complete imagined transitions without generating intermediate
video frames.
After adapting the world model and critic on real rollouts, we improve the pretrained actor through either PPO on imagined rollouts or critic-guided best-of-
$N$
selection. DexWAC surpasses the large-scale pretrained VLA and WAM baselines in simulation and
achieves 75% average success on two real-world tasks, compared
with 45% for
$\pi_{0.5}$
. Its world model is more accurate and faster than video-based baselines, and ablations confirm that learning dynamics and value together improves the policy.

Introduction
Large-scale learning from demonstrations has enabled robot
policies to operate across tasks and embodiments,
offering a scalable path toward general-purpose physical
intelligence
[
2
,
13
,
28
]
. Yet imitating actions alone leaves much of the supervision in these demonstrations unused.
A demonstration reveals not only which action an expert
chose, but also how it changes the
world
[
44
]
and how those changes
contribute to task success
[
48
]
.
Data collection and policy execution also yield suboptimal trajectories, failed attempts, and unstructured play, which are often underused by imitation-based policies.
Exploiting this supervision can help a policy understand
both
what its actions can change
and
which factors matter for the task
[
24
]
.
Recent world–action models (WAMs) jointly predict actions and future observations
[
1
,
10
]
, but use this prediction mainly as an auxiliary objective for policy learning.
Meanwhile, methods to improve pretrained policies often introduce separately trained world models
[
9
,
50
]
and reward or value models
[
18
,
43
]
.
For a generalist policy, these models must themselves generalize across
the same broad range of tasks and embodiments as the policy
[
20
]
.
Pretraining them separately at this scale can duplicate computation and relearn overlapping representations.
It also keeps the predictive and value objectives from jointly shaping the features the actor uses
[
5
]
.
These observations motivate two questions:
Can a single pretraining stage jointly acquire an actor, a world model, and a critic?
And can their complementary objectives constrain a shared representation that improves policy learning?
We therefore introduce
Dex
W

Limitations
Achieving sustained and stable policy improvement in
contact-rich dexterous manipulation remains challenging.
We think difficult credit assignment is one contributing
factor
[
25
]
. The problem becomes more pronounced when optimizing a single policy across multiple tasks, where gradients from different skills may conflict
[
46
]
. Finally, due to computational constraints, we have not yet evaluated DexWAC with large-scale robot pretraining. Its scalability to broader datasets, tasks, and embodiments therefore remains to be established.
7
Conclusion
We introduced DexWAC, an efficient framework that trains an
actor, a world model, and a critic together in a single robot
pretraining stage. The resulting policy and world model are
both competitive with strong pretrained baselines, while the
adapted world model and critic can be directly reused for
model-based policy optimization.
Existing approaches often require the
policy and world model to be pretrained separately at large
scale, making it difficult to determine whether a failure
comes from the optimization method or from differences in
the underlying models and data.
By providing all components
through one shared pretraining process, DexWAC reduces this
cost and enables more controlled investigation of policy
improvement.

papers.title: GP--RL--MPC: Uncertainty-Aware Reinforcement Learning-Augmented Model Predictive Control with Gaussian Process Postdecision State-Value Functions
papers.abstract: We propose Gaussian Process Reinforcement Learning-Augmented Model Predictive Control (GP--RL--MPC), which uses a learned critic as the MPC terminal penalty to account for costs beyond the prediction horizon. Gaussian process regression (GPR) enables data-efficient critic learning from limited, noisy rollouts within optimistic approximate policy iteration (OAPI), with soft updates mitigating policy chattering. A tunable risk coefficient weights GP epistemic uncertainty in the terminal cost, regulating sensitivity to uncertain critic predictions. The postdecision state formulation shifts disturbance averaging offline to account for aleatoric uncertainty from the terminal transition onward. Under matching objectives and admissible actions, a one-step horizon recovers greedy value-space RL. After fitting GP hyperparameters by exact marginal likelihood, we construct a sparse deterministic training conditional (DTC) posterior using inducing points selected by pivoted Cholesky (PC), reducing online evaluation costs as the training dataset grows. In a continuous stirred-tank reactor (CSTR) subject to exogenous disturbances, GP--RL--MPC with an appropriately selected risk coefficient and policy screening reduces the sum of squared errors (SSE) by an average of 80.52% relative to an otherwise matched baseline MPC across five random seeds (sample standard deviation: 3.48%).

Abstract
This paper considers model predictive path integral (MPPI) control for nonlinear finite-horizon optimal control problems with bounded inputs, allowing nonconvex and nonsmooth costs. We prove theoretical guarantees that quantify the suboptimality caused by positive temperature and finite sampling on MPPI and establish their implications for closed-loop guarantees. Specifically, we derive a suboptimality bound for infinite-sample MPPI that characterizes the effects of temperature and prior coverage, followed by a high-probability finite-sample approximation error bound that reveals the dependence on sample size, temperature, and cost variability. By incorporating these bounds into a terminal-constraint-free MPC framework, we further establish semi-global practical recurrence of the closed-loop system. Numerical examples involving a four-link planar manipulator illustrate the temperature–sampling tradeoff and the influence of prior quality on approximation accuracy and closed-loop performance.

Introduction
Model predictive control (MPC) is widely used across engineering applications due to its ability to optimize predicted performance while explicitly accounting for constraints
(
Borrelli et al., 2017
)
. However, applying MPC to complex dynamical systems remains challenging, particularly when nonlinear dynamics, nonconvex objectives, and nonsmooth phenomena such as contact and hybrid transitions arise. Conventional nonlinear optimization methods, including SQP
(
Sideris and Bobrow, 2005
)
, interior-point methods
(
Wächter and Biegler, 2006
)
, and iLQR/DDP
(
Li and Todorov, 2004
;
Tassa et al., 2012
)
, typically exploit derivatives or local smooth approximations. While effective for many problems, their performance can be sensitive to nonconvexity and nonsmoothness, motivating optimization approaches with fewer structural requirements.
Among these approaches, model predictive path integral (MPPI) control has attracted increasing attention
(
Honda, 2026
)
. MPPI evaluates sampled control sequences through forward simulations, assigns importance weights based on their trajectory costs, and computes a cost-weighted control update
(
Williams et al., 2017
)
. By relying on trajectory evaluations rather than derivatives, MPPI offers flexibility for nonlinear, nonconvex, and nonsmooth optimal control problems without requiring explicit differentiation through the dynamics. Moreover, its independent rollouts are naturally parallelizable, enabling efficient implementation on GPUs
(
Williams et al., 2017
)
. These advantages have motivated applications in autonomous driving
(
Williams et al., 2018
)
, aerial vehicles
(
Minařík et al., 2024
;
Zhai et al., 2026
)
, trajectory planning
(
Chen et al., 2026
;
Hori et al., 2026
)
and locomotion
(
Xue et al., 2025
;
Schramm et al., 2026
)
, as well as numerous methodological extensions
(
Honda et al., 2024
;
Tao et al., 2022
;
Rabiee and Hoagg, 2025
;
Yin et al., 2023
;
Mohamed et al., 2025
;
Vahs et al., 2026
)
.
Despite its empirical success, existing theoretical guarantees for MPPI remain fragmented. Existing analyses can be broadly divided into two directions with distinct limitations. (1) The first studies MPPI from an optimization perspective assuming infinite samples. CoVO-MPC
(
Yi et al., 2024
)
establishes linear contraction for infinite-sample MPPI under smooth and strongly convex costs.
(
Homburger et al., 2025
)
analyzes infinite-sample MPPI in a smooth, unconstrained setting with a unique optimizer, showing asymptotic first- and second-order control and value suboptimality in the temperature as it vanishes.
(
Fazlyab et al., 2026
)
interprets MPPI as preconditioned gradient descent on a
KL-regularized cost and establishes descent and stationarity
for the infinite-sample MPPI.
(
Wang et al., 2026
)
interprets MPPI as an expectation–maximization (EM) algorithm and establishes asymptotic convergence of repeated, infinite-sample MPPI updates to the optimum. While these studies provide important insi

Conclusions
This paper investigated the suboptimality, sample complexity and closed-loop guarantees of MPPI under finite sample and positive temperature, with suboptimality guarantees established under local Lipschitz continuity without requiring convexity or differentiability. The analysis reveals an important tradeoff: reducing the temperature improves approximation of the original optimum but increases the sample complexity. The sampling distribution and its coverage of near-optimal solutions therefore play a critical role in MPPI performance. By incorporating these approximation errors into the MPC value-function decrease, semi-global practical recurrence can be established under appropriate parameter selections. Numerical results illustrate these effects and the importance of prior quality. Future work will consider model uncertainty and stronger stability results.

papers.title: Reconfiguring Procedural Knowledge for Compositional Robot Skill Adaptation
papers.abstract: General-purpose behavior models increasingly internalize broad procedural knowledge during training, making their adaptation to new goals and skill interfaces less a problem of learning entirely new behaviors than of reconfiguring existing competence. We study this capability as reconfigurability, the ability to realize new behaviors by cost-efficiently restructuring existing components and relations under sparse governing information, where task specifications provide high-level goals and procedure specifications expose a limited set of reusable factors, leaving the concrete bindings and compositions required for execution underdetermined. We propose RecPo, a framework that represents skills task-agnostically through multiple procedure views and materializes executable skill sequences by composing stored transitions to realize task-specific changes. RecPo maintains a procedure knowledge base of skill-induced transitions, with each view exposing a reusable factor and preserving local skill connectivity. At deployment, it interprets task specifications through the same views and resolves the resulting compositional queries over the stored relations to bind skills for execution. On long-horizon tasks in an extended Franka Kitchen benchmark, RecPo achieves 91.9% ordered completion with 1.0 ms of task inference per episode across varying procedure support and task-record sparsity. Real-robot studies further demonstrate adaptation through local memory edits without task-specific retraining.

papers.title: Task Convergent Flow Matching for Generative Robotics
papers.title_zh: 面向生成式机器人学的任务收敛流匹配
papers.abstract: Successful manipulation requires the manipulated objects to progress toward a desired task outcome. Generative policies can produce plausible robot motions without ensuring this progress, allowing successive action chunks to stall or undo earlier changes to the scene. We introduce a task-centric inference-time refinement framework for flow matching policies that evaluates candidate action chunks through parallel physics-based rollouts and searches for motions satisfying sufficient conditions for task convergence. Task-level performance funnels bound temporary regressions while requiring net progress over each chunk. We establish sufficient conditions under which repeated funnel satisfaction yields convergence throughout execution, and use interval-wise Lipschitz bounds to verify continuous-time funnel satisfaction from sampled rollouts. To accommodate contact-rich hybrid dynamics, we refine the flow's source seeds using derivative-free Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy (CMA-ES), constrained to radial quantile bands of the source distribution to help retain the learned motion prior. This formulation supports both Euclidean and pose-valued Riemannian Flow Matching (RMFM) policies. On PushT and three-cube stacking, refinement raises success from 31.3% to 88.5% and from 77.0% to 86.0%. On PushT, whose coverage score responds continuously to the motion of the block, a learned funnel lowers the average maximum loss of achieved progress by 19% relative to constraining the endpoint of each chunk alone, at a similar success rate. With the radial band, 11.3% of the executed motion windows are out of distribution, a rate within the range of held-out demonstrations, compared with 34.1% for an unconstrained search.

Abstract
Successful manipulation requires the manipulated objects to progress toward a desired task outcome. Generative policies can produce plausible robot motions without ensuring this progress, allowing successive action chunks to stall or undo earlier changes to the scene. We introduce a task-centric inference-time refinement framework for flow matching policies that evaluates candidate action chunks through parallel physics-based rollouts and searches for motions satisfying sufficient conditions for task convergence. Task-level performance funnels bound temporary regressions while requiring net progress over each chunk. We establish sufficient conditions under which repeated funnel satisfaction yields convergence throughout execution, and use interval-wise Lipschitz bounds to verify continuous-time funnel satisfaction from sampled rollouts. To accommodate contact-rich hybrid dynamics, we refine the flow’s source seeds using derivative-free Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy (CMA-ES), constrained to radial quantile bands of the source distribution to help retain the learned motion prior. This formulation supports both Euclidean and pose-valued Riemannian Flow Matching (RMFM) policies. On PushT and three-cube stacking, refinement raises success from 31.3% to 88.5% and from 77.0% to 86.0%. On PushT, whose coverage score responds continuously to the motion of the block, a learned funnel lowers the average maximum loss of achieved progress by 19% relative to constraining the endpoint of each chunk alone, at a similar success rate. With the radial band, 11.3% of the executed motion windows are out of distribution, a rate within the range of held-out demonstrations, compared with 34.1% for an unconstrained search.

Introduction
Figure 1:
Generative policy candidates are evaluated through their predicted task evolution, refined against a performance funnel, and executed before replanning from the new scene.
Diffusion and flow matching policies learn multimodal distributions over action chunks, enabling complex manipulation behaviors from demonstrations
(
Chi et al., 2025
;
Rouxel et al., 2024
;
Black et al., 2025
)
. Yet plausible motions do not by themselves ensure task completion: successive chunks can stall or undo earlier progress. For example, a robot folding a shirt may generate plausible grasping and sweeping motions while repeatedly disturbing an earlier fold. Progress must therefore be assessed through the evolution of the manipulated objects, whose desired arrangement defines completion even when many robot configurations are compatible with it.
Existing methods refine generative plans at inference time to satisfy safety and feasibility constraints, using barrier functions or constrained sampling
(
Xiao et al., 2025
;
Zhang et al., 2025
)
. Stability-oriented methods also guide generation or constrain learned motion dynamics through conditions that encourage or require a Lyapunov function to decrease at each step
(
Mizuta and
Leung, 2024
;
Pérez-Dattari et al., 2026
)
. These approaches address collision avoidance, admissible trajectories, and convergence of robot motion. Such requirements do not by themselves ensure that successive action chunks advance the manipulated objects toward task completion.
A recent line of work instead evaluates and refines generated actions through their consequences predicted by learned world models
(
Qi et al., 2026
;
Du and Song, 2025
)
. Task-oriented objectives include predicted progress or distance to a goal at the end of a chunk or planning horizon
(
Yan et al., 2026
;
Hegde et al., 2026
)
, as well as accumulated rewards and terminal value estimates
(
Hamel, 2026
)
. T

Conclusion, Limitations, and Future Work
We presented a task-centric inference-time refinement framework for flow matching policies, which evaluates candidate action chunks through parallel physics-based rollouts and searches the flow’s source seeds for motions that satisfy sufficient conditions for task convergence. These conditions take the form of task-level performance funnels, which accommodate the temporary regressions that manipulation often requires while asking for net progress over each chunk, so that their repeated satisfaction drives task error down throughout execution and can be verified from sampled rollouts through interval-wise Lipschitz bounds. On PushT and three-cube stacking, refinement raises success far above nominal execution, as the funnel’s terminal contraction steers each chunk toward net progress, and its transient bound helps retain the progress already achieved on PushT, where the task score registers it. Radial quantile bands on the source keep the refined motion close to the demonstrations.
Limitations and future work.
The quality of refinement follows the quality of the task potential
$V$
, which we design by hand from privileged world state. Learned progress measures are a natural route to perceptual and long-horizon tasks. Refinement also uses the simulator as its world model, so it requires the state of the scene and a simulator whose rollouts predict the executed motion. Learned world models could take this role on physical systems. The convergence results apply to executed chunks that satisfy their funnel, the search can execute a plan that does not, and estimated verification uses rates derived from the samples in place of certified bounds. Finally, planning takes seconds per chunk (Appendix
H
), during which the scene has to stay s

till, so refinement does not yet run in real time. Appendix
I
discusses these points further.

papers.title: Zero-Shot Compositional Generalization for Embodied Manipulation
papers.title_zh: 面向具身操作的零样本组合泛化
papers.abstract: Robot demonstrations are collected on different embodiments, leaving many robot-skill combinations unobserved. Pooling these data shares visual knowledge, while joint labels remain tied to the demonstrating kinematic chain. We propose a geometry-supervised training framework for zero-shot composition of familiar robots and skills. The central insight is that a demonstrated command provides a tool-space target for every robot that can realize it. Calibrated forward kinematics supplies this supervision to foreign native action interfaces without their joint labels for that skill. Native reconstruction retains demonstrated configurations, and positive reachability checks select targets for cross-robot supervision. A visual policy learns to predict shared actions and executes through the target robot's native decoder. During policy learning, one prediction receives geometric supervision through both source and foreign native realizations. Matched supervision controls, repeated policy training and evaluations across three backbones and two simulators demonstrate improved transfer to missing robot-task combinations.

Abstract
Robot demonstrations are collected on different embodiments, leaving many robot–skill combinations unobserved. Pooling these data shares visual knowledge, while joint labels remain tied to the demonstrating kinematic chain. We propose a geometry-supervised training framework for zero-shot composition of familiar robots and skills. The central insight is that a demonstrated command provides a tool-space target for every robot that can realize it. Calibrated forward kinematics supplies this supervision to foreign native action interfaces without their joint labels for that skill. Native reconstruction retains demonstrated configurations, and positive reachability checks select targets for cross-robot supervision. A visual policy learns to predict shared actions and executes through the target robot’s native decoder. During policy learning, one prediction receives geometric supervision through both source and foreign native realizations. Matched supervision controls, repeated policy training and evaluations across three backbones and two simulators demonstrate improved transfer to missing robot–task combinations.

1
Introduction
Suppose one robot learns to place a cup on a shelf and another learns to place containers in a drawer. Each has practiced grasping, transporting and releasing objects. A shared policy has also seen both tasks. Yet asking the second robot to place the cup introduces a missing combination of a familiar robot and a familiar skill. This gap is common when robot datasets are assembled from separate platforms, environments and collection efforts. Collecting every task on every robot scales with the product of the two sets. Reusing demonstrations requires a way for supervision from an observed combination to inform a missing one.
The action labels make this difficult. A joint vector describes how the demonstrating robot moves. Its entries depend on joint count, link geometry, joint conventions and installation. Even when two arms have the same number of joints, equal numerical commands can move their tools differently. A shared model can learn useful transfer from images, language and repeated task structure, but native labels provide no explicit correspondence between these different motions. Padding labels to a common width makes them compatible with a network input or output. The remaining learning problem is to connect their physical meanings.
Known robot geometry supplies a physical correspondence. A demonstrated joint command determines the calibrated tool’s position, orientation and opening in a shared task frame. For another robot, this target constrains the effect of its action while leaving its joint solution to its own kinematic chain. One source demonstration can therefore supervise several native action interfaces, including those without demonstrations of the source task. The required information is the robots’ geometry and calibration, together with evidence that a foreign chain can reach the target. Figure
1
illustrates how this supervision can connect familiar robots and skills across missing combinations.
Our approach learns native action interfaces around this supervision path. A source action is encoded into shared coordinates and decoded by both its own interface and a foreign robot’s interface. Native reconstruction anchors each robot to its de

Discussion and Conclusion
Calibrated geometry lets a source demonstration supervise native action realizations across robots. The same relation trains action interfaces and guides policy predictions through their frozen decoders. Matched comparisons across backbones and simulators demonstrate improved transfer to missing robot–task combinations.

Second, we supervise policy predictions through source and eligible foreign realizations using the same demonstration-derived tool targets. papers.title: Hidden Variables Behind Real-Robot Data Quality: Lessons from Hundreds of Thousands of Hours
papers.title_zh: 真实机器人数据质量背后的隐藏变量：数十万小时的经验教训
papers.abstract: As real-robot data collection scales, collection-system design shapes both operator efficiency and the behaviors learned by robot policies. Workspace limitations, control-interface friction, and latency can introduce pauses, detours, and corrective motions into otherwise successful demonstrations. We investigate these effects across embodiment, teleoperation control, and data consistency, combining a kinematic study of 25 dual-arm robots, controlled teleoperation experiments, and real-robot evaluation of fine-tuned $π_{0.5}$ policies. The embodiment study shows that positional reachability overstates orientation-aware task coverage and that modest shoulder motion can substantially expand the effective workspace. Teleoperation experiments show that parallelizing body-part control reduces task completion time by 43-53%, while compliant control improves success and reduces peak contact forces on constrained and contact-rich tasks. Policy-learning experiments show that demonstrations must capture the visual information underlying action choices: active-search demonstrations improve arm-selection accuracy from chance (50%) to 100%. Calibration experiments reveal that mixed-calibration training data remain usable in our tested configurations when an inference-aligned subset is retained, whereas inference-time miscalibration causes all 30 trials to fail. Policies also retain approximately 90% of the extra path length in detour-contaminated demonstrations, showing how inefficient operator motions persist in learned behavior. Together, these findings connect collection-system design to demonstration quality and downstream policy execution. They motivate evaluating effective workspace, control efficiency, observation completeness, calibration alignment, and motion quality before scaling collection, and addressing system-induced compensations at their source.

Abstract
As real-robot data collection scales, collection-system design shapes both operator efficiency and the behaviors learned by robot policies. Workspace limitations, control-interface friction, and latency can introduce pauses, detours, and corrective motions into otherwise successful demonstrations. We investigate these effects across embodiment, teleoperation control, and data consistency, combining a kinematic study of 25 dual-arm robots, controlled teleoperation experiments, and real-robot evaluation of fine-tuned
$\pi_{0.5}$
policies. The embodiment study shows that positional reachability overstates orientation-aware task coverage and that modest shoulder motion can substantially expand the effective workspace. Teleoperation experiments show that parallelizing body-part control reduces task completion time by 43–53%, while compliant control improves success and reduces peak contact forces on constrained and contact-rich tasks. Policy-learning experiments show that demonstrations must capture the visual information underlying action choices: active-search demonstrations improve arm-selection accuracy from chance (50%) to 100%. Calibration experiments reveal that mixed-calibration training data remain usable in our tested configurations when an inference-aligned subset is retained, whereas inference-time miscalibration causes all 30 trials to fail. Policies also retain approximately 90% of the extra path length in detour-contaminated demonstrations, showing how inefficient operator motions persist in learned behavior. Together, these findings connect collection-system design to demonstration quality and downstream policy execution. They motivate evaluating effective workspace, control efficiency, observation completeness, calibration alignment, and motion quality before scaling collection, and addressing system-induced compensations at their source.

Overview.
Operators collect demonstrations through a range of human interfaces (left); the resulting data (center; 200K+ collection hours across 20K+ tasks) train policies across robot embodiments (right). We study three factors that shape these data: embodiment (§
2

Introduction
As real-robot data collection continues to scale, the design of the collection system becomes increasingly consequential for both collection efficiency and demonstration quality. The robot’s embodiment determines which task poses are feasible, the teleoperation interface shapes how operators execute motions, and the sensing and calibration setup determines how those motions are represented in the recorded data. These system choices influence both the effort required to collect demonstrations and the behaviors that robot policies can learn from them. Understanding their effects is therefore an essential part of building a reliable data collection pipeline.
Consider an ordinary grasping task. The robot may respond quickly to commands, yet the video presented to the operator can lag behind its actual motion. The operator notices an overshoot only after it has occurred, pauses to wait for feedback, and then corrects the trajectory. Limited workspace or frequent control-mode switching can introduce further adjustments. The grasp may ultimately succeed, while the recorded demonstration includes the pauses, detours, and corrections needed to compensate for the collection system.
Task success alone does not reveal the quality of the resulting demonstration.
Some compensatory motions may subsequently be reproduced by a policy trained on those trajectories.
Other data issues arise from the information and coordinate relationships available during collection. An operator may choose an action using visual cues outside the robot’s recorded camera views, leaving the policy without the evidence needed to make the same decision. Differences in joint-zero calibration can cause the same recorded joint values to correspond to different physical configurations across robots or collection sessions. These issues affect different aspects of the learning problem: whether observations support action choices, whether recorded states and actions are consistent, and whether demonstrated motions are efficient.
Demonstration quality therefore requir

Conclusion
From embodiment design through the control system to data quality, our analysis points to a single chain:
the design of the collection system determines how much extra effort operators must spend, and that effort can in turn shape the training data and the final model behavior.
At the embodiment level, the effective workspace should be evaluated in terms of the positions, end-effector orientations, and joint margins a task requires, with waist DoFs and end-effector length configured accordingly. At the control level, body parts should be operated in parallel, compliant control should be chosen for contact tasks, and the full human-in-the-loop path, including visual feedback, should be optimized to reduce waiting, switching, and repeated correction. At the data level, key observations must explain the actions, collection and inference must share a consistent state reference, and ineffective compensatory motions in demonstrations must be controlled.
These findings suggest a practical engineering path:
before scaling collection, validate the embodiment’s effective workspace, the operator’s efficiency, and the data’s learnability on representative tasks.
Beyond task success, record completion time, repeated corrections, trajectory length, and motion continuity, and check data quality through small-scale model training and real-robot testing. Fix the system bottlenecks these reveal first, then scale up collection.
Scaling collection requires continually raising throughput, but also reducing the wasted operations and downstream rework behind each demonstration. Improving the collection system promises to raise both data-production efficiency and the quality of the motions models learn.
Limitations and future work.
Our experiments have limited scope. The embodiment

analysis relies mainly on URDF models, discretized IK, and representative morphologies; real workspaces are further constrained by collisions, dynamics, and hardware limits. The control-system experiments cover a few representative tasks and a limited set of operators and device configurations; other robot platforms and proficiency levels may yield different results. The data-quality experiments focus on specific tasks, a single policy model, and one action representation, and some use artificially injected offsets or a single training run. They reveal concrete data failure modes, but the magnitude and generality of these effects deserve validation on more tasks and policy architectures. Future work will further connect collection efficiency, trajectory quality, and model performance: under the same tasks and collection budget, we will compare data produced by different system configurations and the policies trained on them, forming a complete evaluation pipeline spanning collection, quality inspection, training, and real-robot acceptance.

papers.title: Distilling World Action Models for Efficient Bimanual Manipulation via Anchored Path Matching
papers.title_zh: 通过锚定路径匹配蒸馏世界动作模型以实现高效双臂操作
papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) jointly generate future video and robot actions through iterative denoising. Few-step distillation reduces the number of model evaluations, but its coarse updates can move the student away from the teacher's trajectory. We propose Anchored Path Matching (APM), which supervises endpoint and short-transition predictions from states reached by the student. From each state, we continue the teacher to zero noise and use its endpoint and first intermediate state as targets. Modality-routed adapters learn to match both targets from the same starting state. When the two gradients conflict, anchor-priority updates preserve the endpoint gradient and remove the opposing component of the local gradient within each modality. One checkpoint supports 1-, 2-, and 4-step joint generation. The sampling budget can be chosen at deployment without retraining or teacher queries. On RoboTwin 2.0, we train only on Clean demonstrations and evaluate directly on the domain-randomized Random setting. At one step, APM improves closed-loop success over continued base distillation at matched inference budgets by 2.0 percentage points on Clean and 1.4 on Random. Video peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) rises from 30.169 to 32.317 dB, with gains in structural similarity (SSIM) and learned perceptual image patch similarity (LPIPS). On two real-robot tasks, APM improves success over the one-step teacher and reduces control-cycle latency by $21.3\times$ relative to the eight-step teacher.Project page: https://jialonglong.github.io/Anchored-Path-Matching/.

Recent efforts improve few-step WAM distillation through teacher-guided transitions or endpoint supervision. AnyStep-WAM restarts the teacher from the first recycled preview state to supervise subsequent sampling-budget intervals, while its separate endpoint loss is computed from states along the teacher trajectory

Specifically, coarse student updates can drive generation away from the teacher trajectory, causing the student to encounter states that the teacher would not normally visit. Consequently, local-transition supervision and endpoint supervision may be applied to different state distributions: a teacher transition provides guidance on local prediction dynamics, whereas an endpoint target constrains the completed video and actions. Conclusion and Discussion
In this work, we introduced
Anchored Path Matching (APM)
for few-step World Action Model distillation. By pairing endpoint and local-transition supervision at the same student-reached state and prioritizing endpoint gradients, APM addresses both trajectory mismatch and conflicting supervision. A single checkpoint supports multiple sampling budgets without retraining or teacher access at inference. Experiments on RoboTwin 2.0 and physical robots demonstrate improved closed-loop manipulation and video prediction quality, together with substantially reduced inference latency while maintaining competitive task performance.
The current real-robot evaluation is limited to two manipulation tasks on a single platform. Both endpoint and local-transition targets are derived from the same teacher continuation, avoiding an additional teacher rollout for local supervision. Future work could adapt the correction according to teacher reliability and investigate longer prediction horizons and additional robot platforms.

papers.title: Robust Actor-Critic Learning under Transport and Divergence Uncertainty
papers.abstract: Learning reliable control policies requires accounting for uncertainty in transition dynamics and errors introduced by function estimation and action generation. We develop an actor--critic method for discounted robust Markov decision processes with continuous states and actions and an unknown nominal transition law. We consider transition uncertainty sets defined by Wasserstein distance, total variation, Kullback--Leibler divergence, or Pearson chi-square divergence. A conditional diffusion model is fitted once to offline transitions. At each subsequent iteration, we estimate the robust action-value function from current-policy observations using a shared-target minimax criterion, then update a generative actor through exponentially weighted score matching. Regularization preserves exploration and provides the density regularity needed for conditional distribution estimation. Under coverage and regularity conditions, we establish finite-sample bounds for critic estimation, the learned conditional action law, and the robust return of the implemented policy. The bounds distinguish critic estimation error, uncertainty in the nominal transition model, and policy regularization, and characterize how the four robustness radii affect the resulting guarantees.

papers.tldr: 学习可靠控制策略需考虑转移动态不确定性与函数估计误差。本文针对连续状态动作且名义转移未知的鲁棒马尔可夫决策过程，提出演员评论家方法，采用Wasserstein、全变差与KL等不确定性集合，并用条件扩散模型拟合离线转移数据。通过共享目标的极小极大准则估计鲁棒动作价值并更新生成式演员，提升了不确定性下的策略可靠性。

papers.title: Lyapunov-Inspired Sustained Balance on Dynamically Responsive Supports
papers.abstract: Conventional balance formulations often assume a rigid, stationary support, decoupling body stabilization from support motion. This assumption becomes inadequate on mechanically responsive supports, creating a coupled control challenge: corrective body motions intended to restore equilibrium can also excite support motion. We formulate sustained balance as a coupled regulation problem that coordinates equilibrium restoration with suppression of motion induced by the robot's own corrections. We introduce LISST (Lyapunov-Inspired Sustained Stabilization), a learning framework that accounts for how earlier actions shape the conditions for subsequent corrections. It uses recent observations to support immediate adjustments and longer histories to characterize persistent motion, with physical supervision relating the learned representation to robot-support behavior. To evaluate corrective actions, LISST uses coupled dynamics to assess both imbalance and the direction of motion. A Lyapunov-inspired criterion measures progress over finite windows, accommodating the transients required to restore balance. This physical evaluation guides joint-level policy learning through backpropagation through differentiable model rollouts. Privileged guidance focuses training on difficult states reached by the deployment policy and is transferred through distillation. The resulting policy operates using only onboard proprioception. Real-world experiments demonstrate that LISST maintains balance while limiting residual oscillations during continuous interaction with a dynamically responsive support. Video: youtu.be/iGHU7S4wPyw.

papers.title: Stability-Constrained Imitation Learning for Performance-Guaranteed Neural Feedback Frequency Control in Microgrids
papers.abstract: Guaranteeing performance for frequency control is challenging within traditional control paradigms, as it demands precise disturbance estimation and real-time control signal computation within a timeframe of seconds. This paper addresses this challenge by proposing a stability-certified imitation learning framework for frequency regulation in low-inertia microgrids. Based on the frequency response model of the microgrid, an offline numerical optimal control is employed to generate near-optimal pairs of state and control dataset, which are subsequently used to train a deep neural network (DNN) feedback controller. To ensure the closed-loop stability, the DNN controller is trained with a set of Lyapunov-based stability constraints derived using absolute stability theory. Such an imitation learning paradigm can significantly improve the training efficiency, while the resulting DNN controller acts as an end-to-end function that simultaneously handles disturbance estimation and control optimization. The proposed framework is validated on a modified IEEE 33-node diesel-wind microgrid. The DNN controllers are deployed in wind turbine generators (WTGs) to provide decentralized, intelligent supplementary active power support to always maintain frequency deviations within predefined safety bounds under different disturbances while preserving closed-loop stability.

papers.title: Sim2CBF: From Forward Simulations to Implicit Control Barrier Function Safety Filtering without Model Derivatives
papers.abstract: Failure avoidance in complex robot-environment interactions is challenging because the underlying dynamics are difficult to model accurately, and available predictive models may not provide reliable derivatives. We present Sim2CBF, a failure-avoidance framework that solves the Control Barrier Function (CBF)-Safety Filter (SF) optimization problem using only forward-model evaluations, thereby avoiding differentiation of the predictive model. Specifically, we approximate the CBF constraint using finite differences and local linear interpolation over sampled control inputs while preserving failure-avoidance guarantees. The underlying CBF is implicit and constructed from backup-policy rollouts, enabling the use of expressive predictive models such as physics-based simulators and learned world models. Compared with purely sampling-based SFs, our formulation requires fewer control samples and yields less conservative behavior than direct nominal-backup blending. We evaluate Sim2CBF in simulation, hardware box-toppling, and vision-based control tasks, demonstrating its applicability to contact-rich and learned dynamics, as well as its adaptability to changes in the predictive model.

papers.title: Adaptive Action Horizon Selection via Flow-Field Uncertainty
papers.title_zh: 基于流场不确定性的自适应动作时域选择
papers.abstract: Reliable uncertainty estimates are important for adaptive execution in vision-language-action (VLA) models. Existing approaches such as Adaptive Action Chunking (AAC) estimate action entropy from multiple sampled action chunks, introducing additional inference cost and capturing both uncertainty within an action trajectory and diversity across alternative strategies. We introduce Divergence-based Uncertainty-aware Adaptive Action Chunking (DUAC), a post-hoc method that extracts trajectory-conditioned predictive uncertainty from the vector field of a pretrained VLA. Building on a closed-form flow-posterior covariance formulation, DUAC derives action-level uncertainty scores from a single generated chunk using Jacobian-vector products, without retraining or multiple endpoint samples. DUAC strongly correlates with AAC, while capturing distinct information: AAC measures global dispersion across sampled chunks, whereas DUAC measures local uncertainty around the trajectory selected for execution. Consequently, DUAC is less sensitive to diversity among distinct but valid action strategies. Across LIBERO, LIBERO-Pro, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboCasa, DUAC-based adaptive horizon selection performs favorably among the evaluated methods, combining strong task success with low uncertainty-estimation latency. These results establish the flow vector field as an efficient, trajectory-conditioned source of predictive uncertainty for robot decision making.

Abstract
Reliable uncertainty estimates are important for adaptive execution in
vision-language-action (VLA) models. Existing approaches such as
Adaptive Action Chunking (AAC) estimate action entropy from multiple sampled action chunks, introducing additional inference cost and capturing both uncertainty within an action trajectory and diversity across alternative strategies. We introduce Divergence-based Uncertainty-aware Adaptive Action Chunking (DUAC), a post-hoc method that extracts trajectory-conditioned predictive uncertainty from the vector field of a pretrained VLA. Building on a closed-form flow-posterior covariance formulation, DUAC derives action-level uncertainty scores from a single generated chunk using Jacobian–vector products, without retraining or multiple endpoint samples. DUAC strongly correlates with AAC, while capturing distinct information: AAC measures global dispersion across sampled chunks, whereas DUAC measures local uncertainty around the trajectory selected for execution. Consequently, DUAC is less sensitive to diversity among distinct but valid action strategies.
Across LIBERO, LIBERO-Pro, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboCasa, DUAC-based adaptive horizon selection performs favorably among the evaluated methods, combining strong task success with low uncertainty-estimation latency.
These results establish
the flow vector field as an efficient, trajectory-conditioned source of
predictive uncertainty for robot decision making.

Discussion and Conclusion
Our results show that the vector field of a pretrained flow-matching VLA provides a useful trajectory-conditioned uncertainty signal. Unlike AAC method, which measures dispersion across multiple sampled action chunks, DUAC estimates the uncertainty remaining around the particular trajectory selected for execution. The two measures exhibit strong agreement at late flow times, but differ when multiple valid strategies exist: marginal entropy increases with diversity across strategies, whereas DUAC more selectively characterizes the chosen trajectory. When used for adaptive horizon selection, DUAC achieves the highest observed aggregate success rates in our evaluation and reduces uncertainty-estimation latency relative to Entropy AAC.

II-D
Relation to sampling-based uncertainty
DUAC and AAC measure related but distinct uncertainty quantities. AAC estimates marginal action entropy from the sample covariance of multiple generated action
chunks, whereas DUAC estimates predictive covariance conditioned on an
intermediate state of one generated trajectory. Under the linear
Gaussian flow interpolation, the law of total covariance decomposes
the marginal action covariance into the expected trajectory-conditioned
covariance and the variability of the conditional means across
trajectories. DUAC captures the former component and is therefore less
sensitive to diversity among distinct but valid action strategies.
We provide the complete derivation in

papers.title: Reasoning on Call: Efficient Agentic Robot Control for Long-Horizon Robot Manipulation
papers.abstract: Large multimodal models can support long-horizon robot manipulation, but frequent model calls incur substantial latency and token costs. The central challenge is determining when agent assistance or intervention is needed and whether errors require correcting robot execution, subtask planning, or both. To address this problem, we propose RoC (Reasoning on Call), an efficient framework that coordinates a low-level policy and a high-level reasoning agent through an online task-state monitor. The monitor combines temporal visual observations with ordered interaction memory to jointly estimate progress within the active subtask and predict its successor. These predictions guide event-triggered agent review for coordinated execution repair and plan revision. Verified outcomes govern memory updates and subtask transitions, allowing routine execution to remain with the policy while reasoning focuses on decisions requiring additional assessment. On RMBench, RoC improves task success rate by 24.0 percentage points and reduces token consumption by 65.3% compared with the strongest agent-based baseline. It also outperforms the strongest policy-based baseline by 15.1 percentage points in task success rate. Real-world experiments further validate its effectiveness across three long-horizon manipulation tasks. Overall, RoC supports efficient agent intervention and coordinated recovery across execution and planning for long-horizon robot manipulation.
